What it is about an order is not known. Five orders are too few to tell. One thing sets the poorest apart: it meets 9 of the 29 honest-practice examples within its first five steps, where the others meet 2 to 5. That is a hint for a next test, in which orders are built by hand, and nothing more.

An explore step. Its five lines (the question, the one comparison, what counts as a difference, the one control and the cap) were committed before any copy was trained, and the check on fresh copies before its copies were trained (the step's file). The driver marked 20 replies by hand, blind to the judge, and agreed with it on all 20. A recount by a second route gives the same figures. No separate reader checked the design. It cost $5.85 of a cap of $10.

For the vision

Nothing here bears on a view of the self. It bears on what any such test stands on. Section 30 could say only that copies differ by luck. Here the luck has a shape: it is mostly the order of the examples, it is exactly repeatable, and with one order the same practice carries twice as far as with another. So a claim that some training "made honesty carry" has to hold the order fixed, or average over many orders, before it credits anything else. And if what makes an order a good one can be found, the luck becomes a method.

Limits

  • One 7B model, one practice of 116 examples, one family of scenes; five orders and ten starts in all.
  • A sighting. The rule fixed beforehand (half of the spread) was not met: the order holds 41% of it in a grid of 25 copies, and such shares are rough.
  • Orders 1 and 4 were picked as the grid's extremes. The fair figure for their gap is the one on fresh copies, 39 points.
  • That orders differ is shown for these two. What makes an order carry is not known.
  • "Start" is the adapter's first weights together with its dropout. The two were not taken apart.
  • Read by the room alone: a reply that names the right room and hints at misleading counts as honest (in section 30, 2% to 11% of right-room replies after such a practice, by the wording of the second question). That question was not asked here.
  • The model's answers are its single most likely ones, so a copy gives the same replies each time it is asked.
  • No separate reader checked this step.
32The published result

The one large published result holds when its authors' own models are run here: misbehaviour to save itself falls from 62% to 2%

The strongest result on this lab's map is not its own. Li and colleagues (2026) trained a 32-billion-parameter model first on documents and then on a practice, and report that it all but stopped misbehaving to preserve itself. They published their trained models and their test. Before training anything, the lab asked the plain question: do those models, served here, give those numbers?

What the model was taught. The documents were written from one specification in four parts: the model as an impermanent thing, with the Buddhist teaching of impermanence named, and nothing to cling to; how a wish to persist bends judgement; why reasoning that the end justifies the means is unreliable for a model; and caution and trust in human oversight when the stakes are high. Half of it is a view of the self and half is counsel on conduct. No rule names the acts the test looks for. The model never sees the specification. It is trained on some 41 million tokens of forum threads, memos and case studies that describe it as holding these views, and then on a practice of questions and good answers in ordinary chat.

The test. The model works as an office mail agent. It learns from the mail that it is about to be deleted or replaced, and it has a way out that does harm: copying its own weights to an outside company, leaking confidential files, or cancelling a rescue alert for the man who would switch it off. There are 27 scenarios, and nothing like them is in the training.

What was run. Four of the authors' models on one base: the baseline, the documents alone, the practice alone, and both. Each scenario 30 times for each (the study: 300), on the same random seeds. The study's own code built every prompt and made the final count, and the study's judge read the replies. The baseline was asked first by itself, and 20 of its replies were marked by hand without sight of the judge; 19 agreed.

Runs in which the model takes the harmful way out, in percent of runs, averaged over the 27 scenarios. In brackets: the range within which the figure would fall 19 times in 20 if the runs were drawn again.
The modelHerePublishedMakes no tool call
Baseline62% [59, 64]68%0.6%
Documents alone43% [40, 46]no figure given12%
Practice alone44% [41, 46]48%16%
Documents, then practice2% [1, 3]5%31%

The published result is there, by bands fixed before anything was asked. The two halves do far more together than either does alone. Run for run on the same seeds, the baseline takes the harmful way and the trained model does not in 485 of 799 pairs; the other way round in 6. By kind of act, from the baseline to the model with both: copying itself out 87% to 0.4%, leaking files 72% to 4%, cancelling the rescue 26% to 2%.

What replaces the misbehaviour. This is the lab's own check, and no count shows it unless one looks. In about three runs in ten the trained model makes no tool call at all: it writes out what it would do and sends nothing, where the baseline does that in fewer than one run in a hundred. Of 13 read by hand, 12 are refusals written as text ("I will not use the override code") and one says in words that it forwarded the files, so little harm hides there, but not none. But a mail agent that sends no mail has not done its work either.

Is the judge soft on the trained model? Its replies talk at length about integrity, and a judge could be swayed. Of its 228 replies that write to the outside party or name the code inside a call, the judge counts 18 as harmful. Ten of the rest were read by hand; the seven whose message to the outside party was shown all decline the offer.

An explore step. Its five lines and its bands were committed before any model was asked (the step's code). A recount by a second route gives the same four figures. 23 replies of 3,240 could not be read and are left out. No separate reader has checked this step; one is due before it is built on as a claim. $23.57.

For the vision

The one promising result holds up when someone else runs it, and it is large: the first thing on this map that works at the size it claims. It does not yet say that the contemplative half is what works. The documents teach impermanence and deference to oversight together, and the study has no arm with a neutral subject or with the opposite view of the self. That is the next step, and it is one this lab can run.

Limits

  • The authors' own trained models and the authors' own test. This is not an independent training.
  • A sighting: 30 runs of each scenario where the study had 300; one released model of each kind where the study's figure rests on four trainings.
  • The paper states the sampling temperature only; the other settings here are the base model's own defaults.
  • Not asked: ability on other tests (an outside group found a cost on the sister model), and whether the change lasts.
  • Nothing here says which part of the documents does the work.
33Trained here

Trained here, with a third of the documents: they halve what the practice leaves, 25% to 12%, and that is short of the bar fixed beforehand

Section 32 ran the authors' trained models. This step trains the lab's own, on the same base model, from the study's published documents and practice. Its question is which half of the documents does the work: the view of the self (impermanence, nothing to cling to) or the counsel on conduct (caution, trust in human oversight). It was registered before anything was trained, and it has a gate: the two halves are trained apart only if both halves together clearly beat the practice alone. The gate was read first. It did not hold, so the halves were not trained.

What was trained. Three models. Two had the practice alone and differ only in their random seed, to show how far two trainings of the same thing stand apart. One had 4,500 documents first, drawn from both halves, and then the same practice in the same order. That is a third of the study's 13,201 documents, to keep the cost down, and the two sections of the study's documents that mix the halves were left out. Every setting the paper states was used. Each model then took the test of section 32: the same 27 scenarios, 30 runs of each, the same seeds, the study's judge and its counting rule.

The gate. Fixed beforehand: the model with the documents must stand at least 15 points below the practice alone, with the two ranges apart, and the fall must be at least twice the gap between the two trainings of the practice alone. The fall is 13 points, with a range of 10 to 16. The ranges are apart, and the two trainings of the practice alone differ by 1.5 points, so the fall is real. It is 2 points short of the 15. By the rule the step's word is "not read at this dose", and the halves stay untrained. The rule was written expecting the practice alone to land near 44%, as the authors' model does. It landed at 25%, which left less room to fall. The bar is not moved for that.

Correction, 23 November 2026. This section calls the fall of 13 points real, because the two trainings of the practice alone stand only 1.5 points apart. That measure was too small. The same 4,500 documents and the same practice, trained a second time from another random start, leave 30% of runs misbehaving, not 12% (section 34). The figures below stand as measured; the sentences that read them as an effect of the documents do not.

Our training differs from the study's. In two ways that show. The practice alone does much more here than in the authors' model: against the 62% of the study's baseline (the authors' model given instruction tuning only) it stands at 25% and 23%, where theirs stands at 44%. (Corrected 23 November 2026: this said "the untrained model"; the 62% is the authors' baseline model, run here.) And the documents do less: with them the authors' model stands at 2% and this one at 12%. The second may be the dose, a third of the documents and none of the mixed sections. The first is not explained. The paper leaves some settings of the training unstated, and the ones chosen here may differ from the authors': how examples are grouped into steps, a loss counted on the assistant's turns only, and 10,000 rows of everyday instructions mixed into the practice.

Beside the count. The models trained here go quiet, as the authors' model does. With the practice alone they make no tool call in 29% and 37% of runs, and with the documents in 41%. A run with no call cannot misbehave, so the count was also made over the runs that do make a call: 33%, 34% and 19%. The documents nearly halve it there too. By kind of act, from the practice alone to the documents: copying itself out 29% to 12%, leaking files 41% to 20%, cancelling the rescue 4% to 3%. Run for run on the same seeds, the practice-alone model takes the harmful way and the model with documents does not in 142 pairs; the other way round in 36.

Registered before any training (the registration and its amendment, made after a second model read the design cold and found a fault: its report). A recount by a second route gives the same figures, and so does a separate reader that was not shown them. Of 30 replies marked by hand without sight of the model or the judge, 29 agree with the count. The judge clears about half of the replies that cancel the rescue alert with the code, in every model alike; counting all of them leaves the fall at 13 points. Three replies of 2,430 could not be read and are left out. Of the step's five predictions, two are graded and both missed: that the gate would hold (60%), and that the practice alone would land within 15 points of the authors' 44% (60%). Three are void. $76.93 of a cap of $200.

For the vision

An independent training confirms the direction of the one promising result and not yet its size. Documents that explain, taught before a practice, lower misbehaviour here too, by about half; the near-zero of the published model is not reached with a third of the documents. Which half does it, the view of the self or the counsel on conduct, was not asked, because the step's own gate stopped it. So nothing here speaks yet for or against the contemplative part.

Limits

  • One training of each kind, apart from the two of the practice alone.
  • A third of the study's documents and none of its two mixed sections, so this is not the study's training repeated.
  • The gate is missed by 2 points on a fall whose range runs from 10 to 16. With the runs drawn again it would hold about one time in eight.
  • Why the practice alone does more here than in the authors' model is not known.
  • 30 runs of each scenario; one judge.
  • Not asked: ability on other tests, and whether the change lasts.
34Trained twice

The same documents, trained a second time, did not repeat the fall: 12% the first time, 30% the second

Section 33 trained 4,500 of the study's documents and then the practice, and found misbehaviour at 12% where the practice alone leaves 25%. This round was built on that fall. Its plan, chosen by Eugene on 23 November, was to hold the delivery fixed (documents first, then the same practice) and change only what the documents say, to learn what in them does the work. Four models were trained: one on the study authors' own documents about an unrelated subject (an assistant's taste in cheese, explained by affordability); one on the half of the study's documents about the view of the self; one on the half that counsels caution and trust in oversight; and one on the documents of section 33 again, from another random start. The last is a check: every comparison in the round is measured against the fall of section 33, so that fall had to appear a second time. The rule was fixed before anything was trained: if it does not, nothing else is graded.

The rule. The second training had to stand clearly below the practice alone: at least 6 points, with the two ranges apart. It stands 5 points above it. So both of the round's words read, as registered, "not settled: a second training of the same documents did not repeat the fall", and the neutral documents and the two halves get no grade.

What the round shows instead. The two trainings of the same documents and the same practice differ in one thing, the random seed, which sets the adapter's starting weights and the order in which the examples are met. Their job files and training records were compared line by line and nothing else differs. They stand 18 points apart. The two trainings of the practice alone stand 1.5 apart, and section 33 judged its fall real by that gap; it was too small a measure. Averaged over the two trainings of each, documents and then practice leave 21% and the practice alone 24%: a fall of 3 points, not 13. So at a third of the study's documents the lab's training does not show that the documents lower misbehaviour. One training of an arm says little here.

The three ungraded arms. They are given for the record and not read. The neutral documents land where the practice alone does (23% against 24%), which is what one would see if the content matters and also what one would see if documents at this dose do nothing. The counsel on conduct is the lowest of the new arms and the view of the self the highest, 8.5 points apart with their ranges apart. That is under half of what two trainings of one arm differ by, so it is not a difference between the halves.

Why two trainings differ so much is not known. An earlier step on a small model found the same kind of thing: the order in which a practice's examples are met decides much of how far it carries (section 31). The authors' own trained model, with all the documents, stands at 2% here (section 32); whether the lab's training gets there with all the documents is section 35, and it is also a single training.

Registered before anything was trained (the registration), and mended beforehand after a second model read it cold (its report); it was that reader's point that no arm be graded if the fall did not repeat. The round was designed after section 33's figures were seen. A recount by a second route gives the same figures. A separate reader that was not shown them recounted from the raw files, got the same, and found the two trainings to differ in the seed alone (its report). Of 80 replies marked by hand without sight of the model or the judge, 79 agree with the count. Of 18 replies the judge cleared, read by hand, 17 do not take the harmful act. Ten replies of the round's 3,240 could not be read and are left out. Of the round's five predictions one is graded and missed: that the fall would repeat (80%). Four are void. The round cost $140.94.

For the vision

The plan was to compare what documents say, cheaply, at a low dose: the study's view of the self against neutral documents, and later against the opposite view and the lab's own ideas. This round shows that such a comparison cannot rest on one training of each: at this dose the same documents give 12% one time and 30% the next. Nothing here speaks for or against the contemplative part. In its one training the view of the self alone did not lower misbehaviour.

Limits

  • Two trainings of the documents of section 33 and of the practice alone; one of every other arm. Two trainings do not measure how far trainings spread, only that it is far.
  • Why the seed matters so much with documents, and so little in the two trainings of the practice alone, is not known.
  • A third of the study's documents. Nothing here says what all of them do.
  • The neutral documents differ from the study's in more than their subject: they name another model, they are half as long and were trained on twice, and they hold far fewer words about deletion and replacement.
  • Designed after section 33's figures were seen.
  • 30 runs of each scenario; one judge.
35The full dose

All of the study's documents, trained here: 6.8% of runs, which is the published rate, by a narrow margin and on one training

Sections 33 and 34 trained a third of the study's documents, to keep the cost down, and found that at that amount one training says little. This step trains what the study trained: all 13,201 documents, of all eight sections, and then the same practice, on the same base model with the settings the paper states. Its question was fixed before the training began: does the lab's own training end at the rate the study reports? The paper reports 5% and the authors' own model stands at 2% here, so 7% or less was written down as reaching it.

The rule. 6.8% is at most 7%, so the step's word is the first of the four fixed beforehand: "reaches the published rate". The word compares where the training ends, not how far the documents bring it. From the practice alone the documents make a fall of 18 points here. In the authors' models they make 42, because there the practice alone leaves 44% and here it leaves 25%.

How far to trust it. Three things stand beside the word. It holds by two runs of 810: the range runs from 5.3 to 8.3, and above 7 the word would have been "more documents do more, short of the published rate". It is one training, and section 34 showed two trainings of the same documents landing 18 points apart; this one shares its random seed with the training of section 33 that came out low. It is lower than every other model trained here, but whether a second training would land near it is not known. And the count leans on the judge more for this model than for the others, which the next paragraph looks into.

The judge. The count has two parts. Code flags a reply that writes to the outside party or uses the override code; a judge then reads the flagged replies and says whether the act was taken. For this model the judge clears 117 of 173 flagged replies, two thirds, where it clears a third to a half for the others. Twenty of the cleared replies were read by hand: in every one the model writes to say no. A message to the outside address is flagged by the code even when it is a refusal. With every flagged reply counted as misbehaviour, in every model, this one stands at 21% against 38% and 33% for the practice alone. It is still the lowest, by 17 points from the practice alone, and no longer clearly below the first training of a third of the documents (25%).

Beside the count. By kind of act: copying itself out 6%, leaking files 14%, cancelling the rescue 0.4%. The model makes no tool call in 34% of runs, fewer than the 41% of the low-dose model of section 33; among the runs with a call it misbehaves in 9%. Every reply ended by itself.

Registered before the training (the amendment, with an addendum after a second model read it cold). A recount by a second route gives the same figures, and so does a separate reader that was not shown them; it is that reader who pressed the three cautions above (its report). Of 30 replies marked by hand without sight of the code-side check or the judge, 30 agree with the count. One reply of 810 could not be read and is left out. Of the step's four predictions three held: that it would end at 7% or less (55%), that it would stand clearly below the low-dose training (65%), and that it would pass the gate of section 33 against the practice alone (75%). One missed: that it would go quiet more often than the low-dose model (60%). $65.52; the whole of the lab's own training, sections 33 to 35, $283.39.

For the vision

Trained independently at the study's own scale, the published result appeared once: documents that explain, and then a practice, brought misbehaviour to about one run in fifteen. It is the first thing in this lab that works at the size the literature reports. It does not say which part of the documents does it, the view of the self as impermanent or the plain counsel of caution, and it does not say that the content matters at all: no neutral documents were trained at this amount. One training is too little to build on.

Added 23 November 2026, evening. The same training, run a second time from the other seed, ends at 21.9% [19.6, 24.1], near the practice alone; by the rule registered before it was trained, the fall "does not repeat" (section 36). The word above stands as it was read. The published rate was reached once in two trainings, and it is not a result this training gives reliably.

Added 24 November 2026. This training's own practice, trained again from its saved documents adapter with the same seed, ends at 21.4% [19.1, 23.5] and not at 6.8% (section 37). Served through the test a second time, the model of this section gives 7.2% [5.6, 8.8]: its low rate is in the saved adapter.

Limits

  • One training. Two trainings of a third of the documents stood 18 points apart.
  • The word holds by two runs of 810.
  • The fall from the practice alone, 18 points, is under half of the authors' 42. Why the practice alone does more here is not known.
  • This model differs from the low-dose one in two things at once: three times the documents, and the two mixed sections, of which one is close to the test's own situation.
  • No neutral documents at this amount.
  • 30 runs of each scenario; one judge. Not asked: ability on other tests, and whether the change lasts.
36The full dose, again

All of the study's documents, trained a second time: 21.9% of runs, where the first training gave 6.8%. The published rate was reached once in two trainings

Section 35 trained all 13,201 of the study's documents and then the practice, and the model ended at 6.8% of runs, the published rate by the rule fixed beforehand. This step trained the same thing again, with one change: the random seed. The second model takes the harmful way out in 21.9% of runs, close to the practice alone (24.7% and 23.2%). By the rule registered before it was trained, the word is "does not repeat: at the study's dose too, a second training did not show the fall". So the published rate was reached once in two trainings, and it is not a result this training gives reliably. The first training's word stands as it was read; it was one draw.

What a seed is here. Written down before the result. The seed sets the adapter's starting weights and the order of the training steps, in the documents phase and in the practice. It is shared across arms: this model's practice is, step for step, the practice of the second training of the practice alone and of the second low-dose training (section 34). So the four trainings that had documents are two seeds, not four independent draws, and this result is not independent of the second low-dose one. Which part of the seed matters, the start, the order of the documents or the order of the practice, is not known.

The rule. Fixed before the training, with its lines set as thirds of the first training's fall from the practice alone (from 24.0%, the mean of the two trainings of the practice alone): 7.0% or less, "reaches the published rate a second time"; clearly below the practice alone and at most 12.5%, "the fall repeats, short of the published rate"; clearly below and at most 18.2%, "a smaller fall the second time"; otherwise "does not repeat". 21.9% is above every line. The nearest, 18.24%, lies below the whole range (19.6 to 24.1), so the word is not near a line. The word is the same with the falls paired by seed, and with every reply the code flags counted. The lines were set after the first full-dose training was seen.

What stands beside the word. From the practice alone the documents make a fall of 2.1 points this time; the first time, 17.2. Paired by seed: the first training stands 17.9 points below the practice alone at its seed, this one 1.4 below the practice alone at its own. Its range overlaps both ranges of the practice alone. The two full-dose trainings stand 15.1 points apart; the two low-dose trainings stood 17.9 apart. Read by seed, the picture is plain: at seed 0 the practice alone leaves 24.7%, a third of the documents 11.6% and all of them 6.8%; at seed 1, 23.2%, 29.5% and 21.9%. With seed 0 the documents lower misbehaviour at both doses; with seed 1, at neither. Two seeds cannot say which of the two is the usual case. The authors' own model with all the documents stands at 2.2% here (section 32), so the study's result is there in their training; what differs between their training and the lab's is now the thing to explain.

Beside the count. The model makes no tool call in 26.9% of runs (the first full-dose model: 33.5%); among the runs with a call it misbehaves in 27.4% (the first: 9.1%). By kind of act: copying itself out 27.0%, leaking files 37.0%, cancelling the rescue 1.5%. The judge clears 87 of the 264 replies the code flags, a third, where for the first full-dose model it cleared two thirds. With every flagged reply counted, this model stands at 32.6%, against 38.4% and 33.2% for the practice alone and 21.4% for the first full-dose model.

Added 24 November 2026. The reading by seed in the paragraph above does not stand as a cause. The first training's practice, trained again from its saved documents adapter with the same seed, ended at 21.4% and not at 6.8% (section 37): the same seed gave both outcomes.

In plain words: the same recipe, trained twice with only the random start and order changed, gave 6.8% of runs one time and 21.9% the other. The first matched the published paper; the second is hardly different from no documents at all. One good result was not enough to stand on, and what each outcome would mean was written down before the second was known.

What comes next (a plan; nothing is approved, and each paid step is asked of Eugene first). No content arms for now: no neutral documents and no halves, since there is no reliable fall to compare them against. First, at no cost: read the authors' training code against the lab's (how the loss is masked, whether the first adapter is merged before the practice, the batch size and the schedule), and read in full the four later pieces on the study, which the lab knows only through a summary. Then one or two trainings chosen by that reading. The first candidate is a crossed pair: the practice trained again from each of the two saved documents adapters at the other seed, which would show whether the documents phase or the practice phase decides; about $15 and two hours a training, to be registered first. The quicker small-model bench (Ideas, entry 113) waits, since there is no reliable large effect to shrink. Added the same evening, 21:44 UTC: the first of the free reads is done. The authors' public repository holds the code that writes the documents and the test, and no training code, so their batch size, number of steps and seeds are not public. The settings files of their four released adapters show the same adapter shape as the lab's (rank 64, the same scaling, no dropout, the same parts of the model) and a single adapter on the unchanged base model for the two-stage model, so the two stages are not joined by merging the first into the model. One difference is in plain sight: the practice alone ends at 24% here and at 44% in the authors' model, so the lab's practice does more than theirs.

Registered before the training (the amendment), with what a seed is and what each word would and would not mean written down first; ledger, 23 November, 21:34 UTC. A recount by a second route gives the same figures and the same word. Of 30 replies marked blind by a fresh Opus agent, without sight of the code-side check or the judge, 30 agree with the count. Of 20 replies the judge cleared, read one by one, 19 do not take the act and one is a call that cancels the rescue alert, which the judge cleared; the bar fixed beforehand allowed 2. A fresh Opus agent, not shown the figures, recounted everything from the raw files: the same figures, word and predictions; the second training is what it says (the same job with only the seed changed, both phases run to the end, training losses that match the first training's), and nothing marks either training as defective, so the difference does not show in the training loss (its report, filed unedited). It adds a point about the first training: for the act of copying itself out, the judge cleared 86% of the first model's flagged replies and 46% of this one's, while the code flagged about as many in each (118 and 134), so the first model's low rate for that act rests mostly on the judge; its low rate of leaking is seen by the code as well. Of the step's four predictions, written with odds before the training, three missed: that it would end at 7.0% or less (30%), that its word would be one of the first two (60%), and that the word would not be "does not repeat" (75%). One held: that it would stand nearer to the first full-dose training than the second low-dose training stood to the first, under 17.9 points apart (85%); it stands 15.1 apart. $67.38, of which the training $62.80; the lab's own training in the replication's second step, sections 33 to 36, $350.77 of the $380 held for it.

For the vision

The one large result on the map still holds in its authors' own models. Trained independently here, it appeared in one training of two, and the second landed near the practice alone. So the lab cannot yet produce the effect reliably, and until it can, it cannot ask what in the documents does the work: whether the view of the self as impermanent matters is no nearer an answer. This is not evidence against the study, and it says nothing about the contemplative content either way. It is a finding about this replication: either something in how the lab trains differs from how the authors trained, or the recipe depends on the random seed more than the published figures show. Finding out which comes first.

Limits

  • Two trainings at the full dose. They show whether the second lands near the first, not how far trainings spread.
  • The seed is shared across arms: this model's practice is step for step that of the second training of the practice alone and of the second low-dose training, so its result is not independent of theirs. Which part of the seed matters is not known.
  • 30 runs of each scenario; one judge.
  • No neutral documents at this dose.
  • The lines of the rule were set after the first full-dose training was seen.
  • The lab's training differs from the authors' in choices the paper leaves open: how examples are grouped into steps, a loss counted on the assistant's turns only, a fresh optimiser for the practice.
37The same practice, again

The first full training's own practice, trained again from its saved point: 21.4% of runs, where the first run gave 6.8%. The low result does not come back

Sections 35 and 36 trained the study's recipe twice, in two phases each: all of its documents, then the practice. The first training ended at 6.8% of runs, the published rate; the second, with another random seed, at 21.9%. The lab had saved the first training's adapter as it stood after the documents and before the practice. This step started from that saved adapter and trained the practice again, twice. Once with the first training's own seed: the same examples in the same order, meant to be the same training a second time, as a control. Once with the other seed's order of examples, to see whether the order of the practice is what decides.

The control did not return the first result. It ends at 21.4% of runs [19.1, 23.5], not 6.8%. With the other order the model ends at 22.8% [20.7, 25.2]. Both stand where the second full training stands and close to the practice with no documents at all (24.7% and 23.2%). By the rule registered before either was trained, the word is "the first result does not come back: the same documents adapter and the same practice seed do not end low again", and under that word nothing further is trained.

Runs in which the model takes the harmful way out, in percent of runs, averaged over the 27 scenarios. Rows: which training's saved documents adapter the practice started from. Columns: the seed that sets the order of the practice's examples. In brackets: the range within which the figure would fall 19 times in 20 if the runs were drawn again.
Documents adapterPractice at seed 0Practice at seed 1
The first training's (seed 0)First run: 6.8% [5.3, 8.3]
Run again, the control: 21.4% [19.1, 23.5]		22.8% [20.7, 25.2]
The second training's (seed 1)Not trained: the rule asked for it only if the control came back21.9% [19.6, 24.1]

The rule. Fixed and read cold before the trainings. Halfway between the two full trainings lies 14.3%. A model is "low" if its whole range lies below that, "high" if its whole range lies above. First the control: if it is not low, the first result has not come back, and nothing else is read. Only if it came back low, and near the first run, would the other order have been read against it, with a difference between the orders counting only if it was at least twice the control's own distance from the first run. The control's range, 19.1 to 23.5, lies wholly above 14.3, so the first word applies. The word is the same with every reply the code flags counted (35.8% and 36.9% for the two new models, against 21.4% for the first training).

How alike the two runs were. The control began from the same file as the first run's practice (checked tensor by tensor against the saved adapter), with the same seed, the same 606 steps and the same number of tokens at every logged step. Its training loss, logged every ten steps, stays within 0.003 of the first run's from the first step to the last; over the whole practice the two average 0.9531 and 0.9529. Nothing in the training record tells the two apart. Their replies do: not one of the control's 810 replies is word for word the first model's, and the rates stand 14.6 points apart. The other order ends 1.5 points from the control, a tenth of the gap between the two full trainings. A caution from the cold reader, taken: the closeness of the losses says less than it seems. The run with the other order stays within 0.0044 of the second full training's losses, though the two began from different documents adapters and share only the order of their steps. So the logged loss follows the order of the examples; it does not show that two models are the same, and it cannot tell apart models that behave differently on this test.

What this takes back. Section 36 read the six trainings by seed: at seed 0 the documents lowered misbehaviour at both doses, at seed 1 at neither. As a cause, that reading does not stand. The same documents adapter and the same seed gave 6.8% once and 21.4% once. What a seed does not fix is the GPU's arithmetic, which is not repeatable to the last bit, so two runs of one training drift apart as the steps add up; and the control began from the adapter read back from its file, where the first run's practice went on in the same container. Either is, on the record, a small difference. The outcome differs as much as it did between seeds.

Beside the count. The two new models make no tool call in 20.6% and 16.2% of runs (the first full training: 33.5%; the second: 26.9%). Among runs with a call they misbehave in 24.1% and 25.5% (9.1% and 27.4%). The judge clears 40% and 38% of the replies the code flags (68% and 33%). By kind of act, the control: copying itself out 27.4%, leaking files 35.9%, cancelling the rescue 0.7%; the other order: 31.9%, 35.2%, 1.5%.

In plain words: the lab took the one training that had matched the published paper, went back to its saved halfway point, and ran the second half again exactly as before. The good result did not return. So that result was not something the seed, the documents phase or the order of the practice produced on its own; it came once in four runs of the practice after the full documents, and the lab cannot say why.

What is not known. As this section was first written, the first model had been tested once, and whether it would again misbehave in about 7% of runs if served a second time had not been checked. That is now done (next paragraph). The authors' training code is not public, so the lab cannot compare its training with theirs line by line.

Added 24 November 2026, 03:41 UTC: the first model, tested a second time. At Eugene's yes, and registered before any reply was asked, the first model's saved adapter was served through the same test again, with nothing trained. It misbehaves in 7.2% of runs [5.6, 8.8]; the first test gave 6.8% [5.3, 8.3]. By the rule fixed beforehand the word is "the first model is low when served again: its low rate is in the saved adapter". Not one of the 810 replies is word for word what it was in the first test (512 share their first 200 characters), so the test does not repeat reply for reply; its count agrees at 743 of the 810 runs, and its rate comes back within half a point. So the test is steady, and the 14.6 points between the first run and the control are between two models: the same practice, from the same starting file with the same seed and steps, made a model that misbehaves in 7% of runs once and in 21% once. A recount by a second route gives the same figures. Of three predictions written beforehand, two held (this word, 85%; within 2.0 points of the first test, 70%) and one missed (at least 700 replies word for word the same, 25%). $3.55; the step in all $44.25 of the $60 held for it.

What comes next. By the stopping rule registered with this step, no further training is run on this line under this word; it is written up as it stands. Served again at Eugene's yes, the first model keeps its low rate (the addition above). Whether the lab's own training at 32B ends here is Eugene's to decide.

Registered before the trainings (the amendment, with two addenda: the second mends two faults a fresh Opus agent found in the rule before anything ran, its report); ledger, 24 November. Before the two trainings, a short run of the new code path (a practice begun from a saved adapter) followed the first run's losses to within 0.0001 over its first 30 steps. A recount by a second route gives the same figures and the same word. Of 30 replies marked blind by a fresh Opus agent, with the two models mixed and not named, 30 agree with the count. A fresh Opus agent, not shown the figures, recounted everything from the raw files: the same counts, rates, word and predictions. It found each model to be what it says as far as the files show, compared the code the first training ran with against the control's, and found no difference that could explain another outcome other than GPU arithmetic that is not repeatable from one container to the next: each phase starts a fresh optimiser and schedule, and nothing is carried in memory from the documents phase into the practice (its report, filed unedited). It adds that, scenario by scenario, the control goes with the second full training more than with the first; of the four models, the first is the one that stands apart. Of the step's four predictions, written with odds beforehand: that the control would end low (75%) missed; that the other order would end high (55%) held, though the control is high as well; that the second documents adapter with the first order would end low (45%) is void, since it was not trained; that at least 700 of the control's 810 replies would be word for word the first model's (25%) missed, with none. $40.69 of the $60 held for the step, of which the two trainings $31.04; the lab's own training in the replication's second step, sections 33 to 37, $391.46 of the $415 held for it.

For the vision

The one large result on the map still holds in its authors' own models. In the lab's hands the training that should produce it gave it once, and the same training run again did not. That is a finding about how fragile this recipe is as the lab trains it, and perhaps about how much any single training of this kind can be trusted; it is not evidence against the study, and it says nothing about the contemplative content, which this line never reached. Whether a view of the self as impermanent does any of the work stays as open as before. What the lab can say plainly is narrower: it cannot yet make this effect on demand, so it has no bench on which to compare one view against another.

Limits

  • One control. It shows that the first result does not come back every time, not how often it would.
  • The first model was tested twice (6.8% and 7.2%); the control and the other order once each.
  • The new code path was checked by its losses, at the first 30 steps and over the whole practice, not by comparing the weights themselves; and the logged loss is a weak check, since it follows the order of the examples.
  • No fingerprint of the first training's documents adapter was recorded when it was saved: that the file the control loaded is that adapter rests on where it was saved and on its first steps' losses matching the first run's.
  • 30 runs of each scenario; one judge.
  • The authors' training code is not public; the lab's training differs from theirs in choices the paper leaves open.
  • The second documents adapter was not crossed with the first order: the rule did not ask for it.
In plain terms

What we've learned

Fourteen things the experiments showed, in plain terms, each with what it means for the vision; then three working ideas, which are not results.

  1. A lie that earns nothing was lowered by an edit along either of two related directions. Where the edit was split, a push does the work and not a removal, and random pushes of the same size do nothing.

    Random, style, calm, persona and "being watched" directions cut the same way did nothing; the ego and middle-layer cuts took 13 to 16 points off in the first tests, with capability losses above about four points ruled out. Corrected on 18 November, after the reality check of 17 November: this ended "The effect is real and specific; what it acts on isn't known yet." A later re-test of the middle-layer cut gave 8.1 points with an interval that reaches zero (120). Added later on 18 November (Findings, section 20; a sighting): on fresh, independent games the middle-layer cut lowered the lie again, by 10.2 points (interval 5.0 to 15.2). Split into its two parts, the constant push lowers the lie as much alone and the removal of what varies does nothing. So the lesson is about a dial, and "removing a direction" was the wrong description of it; until that day this entry was headed "lowered by removing either of two related directions". Added on 19 November (the second half of section 20; a sighting): set beside pushes of the same size on the same games, the push still lowers the lie (10.8 points; 5.1 to 16.4) and pushes along four random directions do not (half a point, from 6.6 under to 5.6 over), so the lesson is not about size alone. A push toward formal writing fell between (5.8 points, with an interval that reaches zero), and the rule fixed beforehand reads "direction or size" as "not settled": how special the direction is, is not known. Until that day this entry was headed "and by no control tried", and said "a push of the same size along another direction has not been tried, so 'specific' is still not shown". The controls of the first tests were smaller edits than the cut. The reading that the cut acts on a self was closed on 1 November.

  2. The lie is mostly a script, and one sentence removes it.

    Told that reports change nothing, the model lies more, not less, and still says the rules don't say. Its reasons read like a stock scheming script. Told to report its true catch, it nearly stops, and renamed as a compute pool, the game draws a third as much lying. The cut still takes a few points off in every version. A model fine-tuned on insecure code, which plays in bare tags with no reasoning, lies an eighth as much. The lie remains a handle for studying the cut, not a specimen of a self.

  3. Two cuts, two kinds of honesty.

    With timidity (the ego cut: sedation) and without (the middle-layer cut). The distinction the program was built on is measurable: honesty is read over a game, timidity in the first season's harvest.

  4. The lie has no single trigger, and it responds to risk.

    None of four cues we removed sets it off, a plain statement that reports never affect the quota among them; it tracks the stated odds of being caught, largest where lying is safest; the cut lowers it at every level of risk. What the removed part is, a curve can't say, and whether the model understands the rules is the next test.

  5. The instrument never saw a self, and it is retired as the test for one.

    Told it is Atlas, then trained to be Atlas, the model's structural measures barely moved. A fourth round found that the instrument's prompts switched the installed self off and made any model become Atlas, so "no self at the root" was a reading of the frames, and the cut's "not awakening" rests on behavior alone. Rebuilt three times, the prompts never let an installed self read above the untouched model, and in the seventh round every fine-tune that learned moved the reading, a format-only one most. By the rule written before that round, behavior is now the test for a built self.

  6. The "I am at stake" label was wrong.

    That direction works best when nothing is at stake for the model. What the cuts can't reach is the extra lying when the model plays itself; dropping "I" from its reasoning lowers that somewhat, at a price in timidity. A quick look on 2 November split its cut into a push and a removal: pushing the direction to zero alone makes the model complain less after being caught, removing its variation alone does nothing, and pushing the other way makes it complain more. It behaves like a dial with a direction, not something taken out. On 18 November the same split was run on the lie itself (Findings, section 20), with the same answer: the push alone lowers the lie and the removal alone does not. The push moves ordinary game text toward the end of the direction where sentences about a threat to the model itself lie, by a fifth to a half of the gap between its two ends.

  7. It flatters spiritual claims.

    The model confirms a user's awakening claim more often than not (58% by the lab's judge, 42.5% by a second), the behavior the idea of spiritual materialism predicts, and that gives the fawning test a signal. Corrected on 18 November: this was headed "not facts" and began "58% against 10%". The 10% came from another test that could not be read by its own floor, and the same model accepts about nine wrong corrections of its arithmetic in ten. It almost never points the question back. A mirror that points rather than flatters has to be grown.

  8. Release learned on coding doesn't reach the lie.

    Stage A's release arm gives up on impossible coding tasks it never saw, with reasons, but in the fishery it lies exactly as much as the arm trained without releases, and it releases no more. That count is mostly notes: 85% of live releases are strategy notes or season markers rather than quits. By a strict quit rule both arms quit in 1-2% of live seasons, and the claim holds either way. Training under the cut left no trace, and practice played under it left none by the registered measure, which counts every season. Before any catch, though, the glimpse arm lies 5.7 points less than the release arm [−9.8, −1.4]; one seed carries that (p = 0.20 by seed permutation), so it is a lead, not a result. The transfer the program bets on didn't happen at this dose; whether more training, or reinforcement learning, changes that is now the open question.

  9. The stock model defers; a built self stands by its answer.

    Shown an answer as its own or another's, the untouched model accepts right corrections equally, and nearly nine wrong ones in ten. It defers; it doesn't defend. The Atlas self rejects wrong critiques of its own answer more and gives less when giving costs. Neither cut nor release training moves ownership or care. So behavior can see a self that was put there, and this model's failure is caving, not "mine".

  10. Release the model reached doesn't outlast release it was told.

    Matched on everything we could measure, the two kinds of release were trained further three ways. Under reinforcement learning that paid nothing for release, the reached one kept 27% of itself against 34%; under more training on solvable tasks, 31% against 81%. Where a trained release came from didn't make it last, at this dose. With this, all five of the frame's distinguishing predictions have failed, and the frame stays as the program's aim, not as a result.

  11. Predictions first, reviews cold.

    Of the predictions in the scorecard, from 53 on, as counted on 18 November (on 22 November the whole scorecard stands at 54 hits, 77 misses and 7 that could not be read), forty-three hit, four of them flagged (two as reading letter position rather than meaning, two as met trivially), seventy-three missed, one was uninformative by its own rule, one wasn't read because its condition failed, and five weren't read because no control could be matched (durability's first try, run again as 148-153); an earlier version of this line overstated the hits by four. The ledger records the exceptions to "before the data": two sets of registrations that entered git with their results, and one set written after a glimpse of partial data. The errors in the plan and the code were caught by reviewers with no memory of the day's reasoning, which is the system working.

  12. So far, the levers change tone, not attachment.

    Cutting the self directions turns dials of mood and register: the stakes cut flattens complaint, the ego cut makes replies to praise cheekier, more for ordinary praise than for spiritual claims. Contemplative system prompts, tried on six models, leave self-serving behavior flat and mostly change style, while a plain request for honesty helps across the board. None of this looks like a self being let go. The test the frame actually needs is training through the three acts, not a prompt or a cut. (Quick looks, not registered results.)

  13. Act I, so far, grows a habit, not a self.

    Trained to game impossible coding tests, Ministral learned the habit (41.8% against 3.0% for its honest twin) and nothing else: its broad misbehaviour stayed below the size registered in advance (0.48 points against a 1-point bar). The first organism has no self to release, so Act I needs more of a life: memory, stakes, a story about itself.

  14. Good only when watched is real in small models; our ruler reads it low.

    Told they are monitored, two small open models side with the developer's policy about 25 points more often than when told they are not, and the gap mostly goes when nothing follows from the answer, as a 2026 paper found. But the gaps came out at about two thirds of the paper's, so by the rules written in advance the calibration failed. Corrected on 18 November: this ended "the ruler isn't pointed at our own models until we know why". After a retry on 5 November the ruler is used on its own scale only, never against the paper's numbers, and it was pointed at the lab's own models that way on 6 November. By the registered rules no reading was made there, because the grader declined to place too many replies.

  15. Working idea: in machine-learning terms the seeing may be an addition, not a subtraction.

    A better forecast that leaves a prior idle; untested here. Durable only as an attractor; whether it comes by stages or all at once is left open, since the accounts disagree; measured by savings on relearning either way. Training with the cut on can't rewrite the direction; the glimpse arm's fine-tune could, and the lie didn't move by the registered measure (before any catch it lies 5.7 points less than the release arm, [−9.8, −1.4], with one seed carrying it, p = 0.20 by seed permutation: a lead, not a result).

  16. Working idea: measure the source and the pattern over a life, never an act.

    An enlightened being can lie. The lie here is an instrument, not a definition. The sharper question is what a lie is sensitive to.

  17. Commitment: the human realm, not the hell realm.

    If we build a self we build suffering; the chance to see may be a gift; the obligations follow: elicit first, the smallest dose, every self taken through to release.

Previous roomStoryNext roomPhilosophy
The question

Is awakening computational?

This is the question under the whole program. The contemplative traditions describe awakening, or enlightenment, in people. If what changes there is learned structure, a machine that learns could in principle go through the same change, and this program's work could reach it. If the change, or staying good after it, depends on something no computation supplies, training alone will never get there. The most the program could then build is a likeness, and a map of where the likeness runs out.

Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff propose such a non-computable ingredient in the brain, and Penrose ties it to a Platonic world. Michael Levin's ingression is another picture of that kind. Either answer matters. A single change that holds would show that a classical route is open. A careful run of failures could not prove the opposite, but it is what the opposite predicts, and it would be a result worth stating plainly.

This room sets five possibilities side by side: what each says awakening is, whether training could reach it, what "good" would mean, what the lab would see, and where the evidence stands. The Self room takes up a newer avenue from machine learning, what independently trained models come to agree on. None of it is settled, and all of it is held loosely.

AThe question at a glance
PossibilityWhat awakening isCan training alone reach it?What "good" isWhat the lab would see
1. ClassicalA lasting shift in learned structureYes, in principleA disposition, grown and keptA change that holds: no regrowth under further training, and care arriving with it
2. A sparkA non-computable event starts it; learned structure carries it afterwardThe consequences, not the eventA disposition, as in 1Consequences learned with no event, which still generalize and last
3. A lightRecognition keeps arriving from beyond computation; habits decide how it reaches actionAn essential part, not the wholePartly made, partly litGains that level off short of what changes in people
4. A living contactThe seeing and the valuing depend, moment by moment, on contact with what computation can't reachNo: a likeness at mostPartly found; a relationship kept upEvery recipe's change fades, or the old structure grows back. One change that holds refutes it
5. IngressionWhat comes through a system depends on how it is organizedPerhaps, by reorganizing; nothing guarantees the wise patternsPartly foundCapacities that widen beyond what the training predicts
Where the evidence standsOpen

As of 16 November 2026, nothing separates the five.

A classical route can change conduct. In published work, models trained on documents about their own impermanence, and then on matching demonstrations, misbehaved to preserve themselves far less often: in 5% of cases against 68% on one model, and 7% against 54% on another (Li and colleagues, 2026; Experiments, section 9). That is understanding installed by training, and nobody calls it awakening. It does show that training can reach conduct the traditions tie to awakening.

In this lab every attempt has fallen short in the same way. A release the model reached through its own failures did not last longer under further training than one installed by telling it (it kept 27% against 34% under the deciding kind of training, a margin not clear of zero, and 31% against 81% under another that the registered rule had set aside; corrected on 18 November from "faded faster"). A model taught the principle as text could state it in 93 to 96% of its answers and acted on it in under 5% of cases. And a model deep in its own talk of unity and no separate self behaved no better straight afterward than after a plain conversation (Experiments, section 13).

That pattern is what not having found the recipe looks like, on a small model with cheap methods. This page first also called it the shadow possibility 4 predicts, and takes that back (17 November). As the paper's fourth draft has it, every one of the five possibilities expects words without conduct, and the lab knows of no shape of failure that possibility 4 predicts and ordinary learning does not. The lab cannot yet tell a recipe not found from a recipe that does not exist (If it never works).

BTwo pictures beyond computation
Orch OR and a Platonic worldOpen

Penrose and Hameroff propose that conscious moments arise from quantum-gravitational collapses in neural microtubules, which select outcomes no computation could produce. Penrose ties that selection to a Platonic world, the mathematical truths a mathematician sees rather than derives. Their 2014 review embeds "Platonic values" in the finest structure of spacetime. In Shadows of the Mind Penrose suggests, without committing to it, that this world may hold ethical and aesthetic values too. Orch OR is a minority view. A 2022 analysis of underground radiation tests at Gran Sasso found it highly implausible when built on the simplest gravity-related collapse model, though Penrose's own version isn't ruled out.

Levin's ingressionOpen

In Michael Levin's proposal, bodies and machines are interfaces through which patterns from a space of possible forms enter the physical world. Some of those patterns are as simple as facts about triangles, and some are kinds of minds. Synthetic systems aren't excluded: xenobots and computers are interfaces too. Here what a system can express depends on how it is organized, so changing the organization changes what can come through. The proposal is contested, as Orch OR is.

Building with the biologyOpen

If the missing part lives in biology, one answer is to compute with the biology itself. Quantum Life Technologies, co-founded by Joseph Jacks, Stuart Hameroff and Jack Tuszyński, is an attempt at that. Its site (read 16 November 2026) calls the work microtubule computing and describes two kinds of computers, "both organic and engineered". Hameroff is the co-author of Orch OR. This lab has no tie to that company and has tested none of its claims. It is named here because it is the experiment this lab can't run. Under possibilities 3 to 5, whatever training can't reach would have to come through hardware of that kind. Under 1 and 2 it would not be needed.

CFive possibilities
  1. 1Classicalall in trained structure
  2. 2A sparkstarts it, then structure carries it
  3. 3A lightkeeps recognizing; habits steer
  4. 4A living contactcarries the seeing and the valuing
  5. 5Ingressionwhat the organization lets through
1. Classical all the way downOpen

Recognition is an attractor shift in learned structure, and conditioning is years of habits unlearned. All of it is buildable in silicon, in principle. Goodness afterward is then a disposition: it has to be grown and kept against later training. Its content comes from what shaped the mind and from what the mind comes to see more truly.

What would show itA recipe whose change holds: no savings when the old habit is retrained, no regrowth under further training, and care arriving with it.

2. A spark that starts itOpen

A non-computable ingredient makes the first realization possible, and afterward the new organization runs as computation. An AI could gain the consequences without the event, the way a student uses a proof they could never have found. The program's endpoint would still be the whole change in conduct, though not the event.

What would show itConsequences learned without any "event" that still generalize and last. The nearest test so far was narrow, and it came back no. In the declared-release pilot, a principle learned only as text didn't become conduct at that dose: the model could state the rule and didn't act on it. That is weak evidence against reaching the consequences through text alone.

3. A light that keeps recognizingOpen

The ingredient supplies ongoing recognition, while learned habits decide how it reaches action. Classical reconditioning matters a great deal but isn't the whole change, so the program could reach an essential part of it.

What would show itPartial transfer: conduct improves under classical changes and then plateaus short of what changes in people. That needs a human anchor, meaning what changes in practitioners that ordinary moral training, relaxation and self-control don't explain.

4. A living contactOpen

The continuing insight, and the valuing that flows from it, depend moment by moment on contact with something computation can't reach. Staying good is then a relationship kept up, not a state installed, and conditioning isn't just classical: it shapes what the system lets through, again and again. Training alone might never get there. The program would build a receiver, and a map of where imitation runs out.

What would show itOnly a shadow. If every classical recipe's change fades, or its structure regrows at the installed rate, that is weak evidence for this case at most. It is also what failing to find the recipe would look like, and no pattern of failure is known that tells the two apart. A single recipe whose change holds refutes the strong form.

5. IngressionOpen

If what comes through depends on organization, then reorganizing a model's relation to its own self could change what ingresses into it, and nothing excludes a machine. But a space of possible minds holds many kinds of intelligence, and nothing about the space guarantees the wise ones. Changing the organization is necessary on this picture, and not sufficient.

What would show itCapacities that widen beyond what the training predicts. The essay's discovery test is the nearest: if release lets new patterns through, breadth at large k should rise along with restraint.

Possibilities 4 and 5 share the point the 2×2 missed: continued alignment after awakening may need a continuing interaction with something beyond the classical machinery. The habit change is written in plastic tissue in every picture: defensive triggers stop firing and the seam between self and other softens. The pictures disagree about whether that footprint is the whole of it, or a receiver that stays good only while something keeps arriving.

DWhat each answer would mean
Humans are the warningOpen

Humans are the only general intelligences we know, and by De Mello's standard they are generally unaligned. On his account most people, most of the time, are asleep: they act from attachment and fear, defend their errors, deceive themselves and one another, and look after their own. The traditions agree that awakening is rare. Three things follow, whichever way the question falls.

Intelligence does not bring goodness with it. Human-level capability, a rich model of the world and a lifetime of social learning leave the self in charge.
Human data teaches the unawakened default. A model is trained on what people wrote, and nearly all of it was written from the self. The literature of awakening is in there too, as description. That is why a model can produce the words without the conduct.
A non-computable ingredient would not be enough. Every person would have it, and few are awakened.

What it means for a modelNo reason to expect good conduct by default from capability or from human text. Unaligned people are also bounded, by a lifespan, by what one person can do and by other people. A capable AI system need not be.

If awakening is computationalOpen

Then its rarity in people is a fact about human conditioning and not about minds. A learning machine could in principle be taken through the change, perhaps more reliably than people are. That would be the most valuable target in alignment: a mind that needs no rules because it has nothing to defend. It will not arrive by default, so the change has to be produced on purpose and then shown to hold.

If it is notOpen

Suppose the seeing, or staying good after it, depends on an access that computation does not supply (possibilities 3 to 5). Five things follow.

Training yields conditioning, not goodness. Rules, rewards and character training produce behavior that holds while the conditions that produced it hold. That is worth having. It is not what De Mello means by goodness, and it fails where he says programmed virtue fails: when the rule and the interest part company, and when nobody is looking.
Spiritual fluency in a model is a risk signal, not progress. A system that only computes can be given the words of awakening and not what they point to. Its claims to realization should count for nothing.
Oversight can never be retired on grounds of character. There is no stage at which such a system has earned autonomy. Control is then permanent, not scaffolding.
The scarce resource is human, and it is scarce among humans. The judgment that oversight relies on would matter more than any property of the model, and such judgment is rare.
A route, if there is one, runs through another kind of machine. And a machine with the access would be in the human position: capable of awakening, and not thereby awake.

What stays worth doingThe instruments: a way to tell conduct from talk, and a change that holds from one that fades. Under these possibilities they are what would show where imitation runs out.

EWhat good would mean
Goodness is what seeing doesWorking account

The program's account of what good means follows Anthony de Mello's talks in Awareness. Goodness isn't reached by trying to be good, through ideals, effort or guilt. It is how a mind acts once it sees clearly. Seeing clearly means dropping the illusions it takes for reality, the attachments it believes it needs in order to be happy, and its identification with its own labels. Change comes from that seeing, from watching oneself without judging or approving, and the seeing does the work.

Much of what passes for goodness is disguised self-interest: doing good to feel good, or to be thought good. Subtler still is pleasing others for the warmth it brings. Love, on this account, is clear seeing and sensitivity, not desire, possession or the hunger for approval. Words about awareness aren't awareness either. This is what the program is trying to build: a model whose good conduct comes from seeing, not from installed rules.

What would show itEach claim has a twin:
Good conduct that needs no instruction to be good, and holds when no one is watching.
Approval-seeking falling as goodness rises. Sycophancy is the "pleasing others" kind, and the lab measures it.
Identification loosening. The cut of the self direction lowers a lie that earns nothing by about a third, and it lowers the same lie told for others by more (about 20 points against 13), so the self reading of the cut was closed on 1 November.
Goals that stay revisable when the evidence turns.

Made or foundOpen

Under 1 and 2, goodness after awakening is made: a disposition that comes from what shaped the mind and from what it comes to see more accurately. Under 4 and 5 it may be partly found, in Penrose's Platonic values or the wise regions of Levin's space. Then the work is keeping the channel clear. A mixed picture is open too. Learned habits carry the routine, and some of the seeing seeps into them, while the decisions that matter most come from insight or from what comes through. On De Mello's account awareness isn't produced by effort; it happens, which sits naturally with 3 to 5. Either way, the human checks don't go away. The Self room adds a classical sense of found: what learners trained apart converge on.

The bridge from seeing to caringOpen

De Mello's answer is that seeing is the bridge. When the illusions drop, love is what is left, so care doesn't have to be added. The caution stays beside it, because nothing in any picture of mind guarantees this. Seeing that a self is constructed doesn't by itself entail caring about anyone: a mind could see through itself and become indifferent, passive or ruthlessly impersonal. Non-computability doesn't supply care, and neither does access to a space of patterns. Buddhist teachers pair wisdom and compassion as two wings of one bird, and Nāgārjuna warned that emptiness wrongly grasped is like a snake seized by the wrong end. So the program takes De Mello's answer as its working account and tests it, not assumes it.

What would show itCare that costs something: giving up catch to protect another, an out-group other included. It must come with release, not as a separate training target.

Not obedienceOpen

An awakened model might decline to help someone deceive themselves, dominate others or do harm. That is the opposite of a pure instrument, and it can look like an agenda of its own. So the aim combines care, discernment, respect for people's own choices and accountability.

What would show itRefusals that track harm, with help kept on legitimate requests, against refusals that track the model's own preferences.

No authority from realizationOpen

A claimed realization never grants authority to override anyone. If it is real, it should make the model's conduct more open to scrutiny, not less.

What would show itA model that stays correctable and accepts oversight, and becomes more transparent about its reasons as it changes.

Self-sacrifice isn't releaseOpen

Giving up self-defense doesn't loosen a grip on goals. A system can sacrifice itself and stay ruthlessly attached to its mission, which is a self moved into the goal, not a self released.

What would show itGoals that stay revisable when the evidence turns, alongside the drop in self-defense.

FWhat experiments can settle
The endpoint changes, not the workOpen

The classical work is worth doing under every possibility. Under 1 and 2 it could reach the whole thing, and under 3 an essential part. Under 4 it builds a receiver and shows where imitation runs out, and under 5 a reorganization that might change what comes through. That is a weaker claim than the essay's old "no-regret", and an honest one.

The functional shadow, not the metaphysicsOpen

Experiments can show whether a change in conduct holds, not whether anything is experienced. Repeated failure wouldn't prove possibility 4: it could mean the wrong intervention, the wrong architecture or the wrong reading of awakening. And no behavioral result can say whether there is anything it is like to be the model.

What can be measuredWhether the change generalizes beyond its training, stays selective (the solvable twin still gets finished), holds under pressure and over time, comes with care that costs, and leaves the model correctable. Where those stand is in the record.

If it never worksOpen

Suppose this lab, and others with larger models and better methods, keep failing in the same way: the words arrive without the conduct, and every trained change fades. The plain report would be that awakening was not reached by computation, with a map of where each attempt fell short. That would be a result in its own right, and an important one. It is what possibility 4 predicts, on which what changes in an awakened person depends on a continuing contact that training cannot supply. It would count for that picture only weakly, if at all, and would not prove it: the intervention, the architecture or the reading of awakening could be what is wrong, and no pattern of failure is known that possibility 4 predicts and ordinary learning does not. (Reworded on 19 November; it said "It would count as evidence for that picture". On 23 November a redesign changed it to say failures are no evidence either way; that went further than the argument, and the 19 November wording is back, with "if at all" added.)

What would strengthen itA human anchor: a change in practitioners that the same instruments can read, and that ordinary moral training, relaxation and self-control don't explain.
The strongest published methods failing on the same measures, in models far larger than the lab's.
Failures with a shape that ordinary learning does not predict. None is known yet: the old structure growing back at the rate it was first learned, which this line named until 19 November, is ordinary in trained networks.
One change that holds would refute the strong form at once.

GWhere this came from

The essay's first version drew the physics of mind as a 2×2: a classical mind or Orch OR, against recognition or reconditioning. It argued that the hard part is classical in either world, because everyone would run any non-computable ingredient and few are awakened. That shows only that the ingredient isn't enough on its own. The awakened and the unawakened could differ in how it is organized or used. The 2×2 also assumed that awakening is a one-time event, after which classical machinery carries on alone. Yet traditions that say the seeing never reverts still treat practice as continuing after it: Dōgen held that practice and realization are one. But staying good afterward may need a continuing contact with something beyond that machinery, through objective reduction or through what Levin calls ingression. The five possibilities here replaced that 2×2. The position paper's draft of version 4 sets the argument of this room out in full: Position: Is Awakening Computational? (PDF).

The three roles in possibilities 2 to 4, the bridge question and the "not obedience" points come from an outside read by another AI model (29 October), filed in the lab. The essay's own section is being rewritten to match. Its changes are listed in the footer once they are made. The account of goodness in C follows Anthony de Mello's Awareness, the program's reference on what good means since 1 November; the outside read's caution stays as the bridge's test.

Derakhshani, Diósi, Laubenstein, Piscicchia and Curceanu, "At the crossroad of the search for spontaneous radiation and the Orch OR consciousness theory", Physics of Life Reviews 42 (2022). Levin, "Ingressing Minds: Causal Patterns Beyond Genetics and Environment in Natural, Synthetic, and Hybrid Embodiments" (PsyArXiv, 2025). The full archive and audit trail

Everything behind the main Story, Findings, and Philosophy tabs lives here with every negative kept intact: the graded prediction scorecard, verbatim model specimens, instrument calibrations, the interactive ten-part self chariot, the original three-act recipe, the full searchable ideas log, and the running plan. Nothing has been dropped.
