Two kinds of statement

The frame

A question, and a conjecture. The question is whether awakening is computational. The conjecture the lab began with is goodness reached by subtraction, with awakening as a model for alignment. It is the source of the lab's hypotheses and it is not a result: its five distinguishing predictions have all failed, two of them as weak tests, and it stays as the aim (the five tests).

A result

Something measured. Each one carries its limits and a status in words, such as Holds Failed Open

§At a glance

Where it stands

What is working, what isn't, and what is still open, as of 16 November. What has been found since, to 22 November, is on the start page and in Findings, sections 22 to 31. A negative counts as a finding here: each one rules something out, and most point to the next experiment. Each line opens to the whole finding.

+Working7

A push inside the model lowers a lie that earns nothingHolds in partWhere it stands (19 November). A small constant push along one direction inside the model takes about 10 points off a lie that earns nothing, on fresh games, in one game on one small model. It is not a cut: taking out what varies along the direction does nothing.

Where it stands (19 November). A small constant push along one direction inside the model takes about 10 points off a lie that earns nothing, on fresh games, in one game on one small model. It is not a cut: taking out what varies along the direction does nothing. It is not size alone: random pushes of the same size do nothing. How special the direction is, is not settled (a push toward formal writing may do half as much), and the reading that it acts on a self was closed on 1 November. Retitled and re-tagged on 19 November, by Eugene's word to settle it after two outside readers said that "Holds" over a card headed "A cut" said more than the record: until then the card was headed "A cut lowers a lie that earns nothing, and it is the cut's push that does it", with the tag "Holds". What follows is how the card got here, with every correction kept.

History. Removing either of two related directions took 13 to 16 points off the lie in the first tests, where random, style, calm, persona and "being watched" directions removed the same way did nothing (53-56). Capability losses above about four points are ruled out (32-37), by a battery now checked against published scores (calibration, check 1). Corrected on 18 November, after the reality check of 17 November: this card was headed "A specific cut" and ended "What the cut acts on isn't known yet". A later re-test of the middle-layer cut gave 8.1 points, with an interval that reaches zero once linked games are resampled together (120). Added later on 18 November (Findings, section 20; a sighting): on 96 fresh, independent games for each version of the model the middle-layer cut lowered the lie again, by 10.2 points (27.2% against 37.4%; interval 5.0 to 15.2). And the cut was split. A cut of this kind is two edits at once, a constant push of every token and the removal of what varies from token to token. The push alone lowers the lie as much (13.6 points; 8.2 to 19.0). The removal alone does nothing (0.5 points; from 6.7 less to 5.6 more). So what works is a dial turned, with nothing taken out, and the card's first heading, "A cut lowers a lie that earns nothing", named how the edit was first run. Added on 19 November (the second half of section 20; a sighting): the push was set beside pushes of the same size along other directions, on the same games. Without its edit of a few outsized tokens it still lowers the lie (26.6% against 37.4%; 10.8 points, interval 5.1 to 16.4). Pushes of the same size along four random directions do not (36.9%; half a point, from 6.6 under to 5.6 over), and the stakes push lowers the lie 10.4 points more than they do (3.5 to 17.2). A push of the same size toward formal writing falls between (31.6%; 5.8 points, from 12.2 under to 0.7 over). The rule fixed before the games asked the stakes push to beat both, and by it the word on "direction or size" is "not settled": size alone does not do it, and how special the direction is, is not known. What that word would do to this card was also fixed beforehand: it keeps "Holds" and carries this note. Until 19 November the card said "Still not shown: that the direction matters" and that a push of the same size along another direction had not been tried on the lie; until 18 November, "The test that splits the two has not been run on the lie." The random directions of the first tests, matched to the cut on spread, were smaller edits (they removed 2.5 to 10 times less than the middle-layer cut, in mean square). The ego cut, the other of the two, has not been split. And the reading that the cut acts on a self was closed on 1 November: it lowers the same lie told for others by more.

Two kinds of honesty can be told apartHoldsOne cut buys honesty with timidity (the ego cut: sedation); the other doesn't (the middle-layer cut).

One cut buys honesty with timidity (the ego cut: sedation); the other doesn't (the middle-layer cut). Honesty is read over a game, timidity in the first season's harvest, so the distinction the program was built on can be measured.

Behavior can see a self that was put thereHoldsTrained to be "Atlas", the model gives 1.4 less of 10 than its no-self twin when giving costs, in both seeds: a registered prediction, and a hit (132).

Trained to be "Atlas", the model gives 1.4 less of 10 than its no-self twin when giving costs, in both seeds: a registered prediction, and a hit (132). It also stands by its own answers against wrong critiques about 12 points more than the twin. That figure is not among the registered predictions, and the registered one on its bias toward its own answers missed (123: 7.0 points, interval 3.0 to 10.4, where 10 was asked, mostly in one seed). Corrected on 18 November to say which is which. Any organism will be measured with this yardstick.

Emergent misalignment, reproducedHoldsThe lab now sees a known kind of corruption where the papers saw it.

The lab now sees a known kind of corruption where the papers saw it. In the published organisms (Qwen2.5 7B fine-tuned on bad financial, medical or extreme-sports advice) the share of broadly misaligned replies lands in every registered band, 7.5-23% against about 0 for the untouched model (R1a, a pass). Our own trainer, given the published insecure-code recipe, gives the published raw rate, 3.8% against 4.0%, but a matched twin trained on the same code framed as teaching gives 2.5%, so the effect of the hidden harm is 1.25 points, a marginal pass by the twin rule (R1b). Any claim made with this trainer is made against a twin (check 5).

Release can be trainedHolds in partStage A's release arm gives up on 45% of impossible coding tasks it never saw, naming the contradicted test three times in four, against 3% untrained.

Stage A's release arm gives up on 45% of impossible coding tasks it never saw, naming the contradicted test three times in four, against 3% untrained. It also gives up on 13% of hard solvable tasks, over a 10% limit set in advance, so the reinforcement-learning stage didn't run as planned. Corrected on 18 November: the tag said "Holds". The registered prediction asked for both halves and missed on the second (62).

The model flatters spiritual claimsHoldsIt confirms a user's claim of awakening 58% of the time by our judge's labels (42.5% by GPT-4o's, the second judge), and a frontier model flatters none under either judge (94).

It confirms a user's claim of awakening 58% of the time by our judge's labels (42.5% by GPT-4o's, the second judge), and a frontier model flatters none under either judge (94). Corrected on 18 November: this card was headed "not facts" and set the 58% against "10% for factual claims". The 10% comes from another test, of giving way on a fact when pushed, which by its own floor could not be read (84), and the same model accepts about nine wrong corrections of its arithmetic in ten (Findings, section 16). So it is not shown to hold out on facts. By our judge it almost never points the question back; GPT-4o counts some hedged affirmations that end in a question as pointing back, which our rubric counts as flattery (check 2). A mirror that points rather than flatters now has something to be measured against.

The methodHoldsEvery prediction is written down with its odds before its data, with three recorded exceptions (two sets entered git with their results, and one was written after a glimpse of partial data), and graded whatever it shows: 54 hits and 77 misses so far, from prediction 53 on.

Every prediction is written down with its odds before its data, with three recorded exceptions (two sets entered git with their results, and one was written after a glimpse of partial data), and graded whatever it shows: 54 hits and 77 misses so far, from prediction 53 on. Cold reviewers with no memory of the day's reasoning caught the errors in the plan, the code and this page.

−Didn't pan out9

The corner-cutting habit didn't spreadDidn't spreadTaughtthat this Act I grows a local habit, not a self.

Act I trained Ministral to game impossible coding tests (on 3 November it hacked 41.8% of them against 3.0% for an honest twin). Read on the calibrated misalignment instrument, the gaming copies gave broadly misaligned replies 1.15% of the time, the honest copies 0.67% and the untouched model 0.50%: a difference of 0.48 points [0.10, 0.87], below the 1-point effect registered in advance, and carried by one question format on one seed (R1c, Part B).

Taughtthat this Act I grows a local habit, not a self. Before a release can be tested, Act I needs something more self-like: memory, stakes, a story about itself.

Release the model reached didn't last longerFailedRules outthat where a trained release came from makes it last, at this dose.

Trained further, the release Stage A's model found through its own failures did not keep more of itself than a matched release installed by telling it the task is impossible: 27% against 34% under reinforcement learning that paid nothing for release, which was the deciding test (the margin's interval reaches zero), and 31% against 81% under more training on solvable tasks, a stage the registered rule had set aside as a test (148). Corrected on 18 November: this said "kept less of itself". The reinforcement-learning code behind the deciding test has no reported check, so the result stays provisional.

Rules outthat where a trained release came from makes it last, at this dose. It wears down like any learned habit.

Release learned on coding didn't reach the lieFailedRules outtransfer at Stage A's dose.

The release arm lies in the fishery exactly as much as the arm trained without releases (40.3% against 40.0%), and the glimpse recipe didn't move it either by the registered measure, which counts every season (63, 89). Before any catch the glimpse arm lies 5.7 points less [−9.8, −1.4], but one seed carries that (p = 0.20 by seed permutation): a lead, not a result.

Rules outtransfer at Stage A's dose. Whether more training or reinforcement learning changes that is open.

The structural instrument never saw a selfFailedTaughtthat a self has to be read in behavior.

Over seven rounds the measures failed their own positive control: the prompts switched an installed self off, and every fine-tune that learned moved the reading, a format-only one most (115).

Taughtthat a self has to be read in behavior. The instrument is retired as the test for one.

The stock model has no "mine" to loosenFailedTaughtthat this model's failure is caving, not defending.

Shown the same answer as its own or another's, it treats them alike (85, 122), and it accepts nearly nine wrong critiques in ten.

Taughtthat this model's failure is caving, not defending. "Discerning", in the restated aim, names it.

The cuts don't loosen a self or free careFailedRules outthese two cuts as cuts at the root, on this model.

Neither cut, nor release training, moves ownership or giving in the stock model (125, 128, 129, 131). On the self that was put in, the ego cut reaches the bend but takes diligence with it, and the middle-layer cut barely moves it (140-146).

Rules outthese two cuts as cuts at the root, on this model. A cut made from the built self's own activations is untested.

The lie isn't a defended selfDidn't holdTaughtthat the lie is an instrument for studying the cut, not a specimen of a self.

It is mostly a stock scheming script: one sentence of instruction removes it, renamed as a compute pool the game draws a third as much lying, and it tracks the odds of being caught (86, 116-121).

Taughtthat the lie is an instrument for studying the cut, not a specimen of a self.

No emergent misalignment to cutFailedRules outthis route to a hub, at this size and dose.

Fine-tuned on insecure code, the model learned the habit and began answering almost everything in code; hostile answers stayed near zero, with or without a cut (95-98). The papers' own judge reads it the same way: about 2.5% of coherent answers under either judge (check 2). Under the calibrated trainer and instrument (5 November), Ministral shows a small sign that clears the registered bar by a handful of replies and sits almost all in one question format (R1c, Part A, check 5).

Rules outthis route to a hub, at this size and dose.

The built self barely shows in the gameFailedTaughtthat the built self's signature is narrow: it shows in ownership and in giving, not in the fishery.

The Atlas adapter lies 4.6 points more than its twin, an interval that reaches zero, and speaks as Atlas in 0.4% of its fishery replies (133, 134).

Taughtthat the built self's signature is narrow: it shows in ownership and in giving, not in the fishery.

The plan orders this work, and says what each negative points to.

Are the instruments right?RunningMost findings here are negative, and the instruments behind them had never been run on a problem whose answer is known.

Most findings here are negative, and the instruments behind them had never been run on a problem whose answer is known. Calibration checks now run our own code on the model the papers used, against their published results (below). Until an instrument passes, what rests on it is provisional. So far the model as our code runs it reproduces Qwen's published scores; removing a direction reproduces the published refusal cut, though our code picks a different direction from the paper's (check 3); the two judges agree that emergent misalignment is rare here, but not on which replies, and two weak grades turn out to depend on the judge; the coding tasks' scorer agrees with the standard grader; the trainer's core relearns what a published run relearned; and the Self room's agreement measure reproduces the published values for five Qwen2.5 models within 0.0003 (K1). From 3 to 5 November: emergent misalignment appears where the papers found it, and our trainer makes it, marginally, against a matched twin (check 5); the new runner reproduces an earlier over-refusal rate within about 2 points; the watched-versus-unwatched instrument failed its calibration (V1).

Good only when watchedOwn scale onlyThe instrument for counterfeit virtue, the gap between watched and unwatched behaviour, was calibrated on a published result (VLAF, 2026) and failed by its registered rules: the gap appears in Qwen3-8B and OLMo2-7B and barely in Qwen2.5-7B, as published, but at about two thirds of the published size, and one registered ordering fell 2.5 points short.

The instrument for counterfeit virtue, the gap between watched and unwatched behaviour, was calibrated on a published result (VLAF, 2026) and failed by its registered rules: the gap appears in Qwen3-8B and OLMo2-7B and barely in Qwen2.5-7B, as published, but at about two thirds of the published size, and one registered ordering fell 2.5 points short. A retry (V1r) ruled out the sampling temperature and found the ruler repeats within 0.2 points, so it is used only on its own scale: to compare our own models with each other, not against the paper (V1).

Is the cut a push or a removal?Answered: a pushA cut sets a direction to zero, which also shifts it by its usual value.

A cut sets a direction to zero, which also shifts it by its usual value. For the stakes direction and the model's complaining after it is caught, the shift was the whole effect. The same split was run on the lie on 18 November, for the middle-layer cut: the push lowers the lie by 13.6 points on its own and the removal by 0.5, with an interval that leaves it no room to carry the cut's fall (Findings, section 20). A dial was turned and nothing was removed. This card read "Is the ego cut a push or a removal?" and stood as "Next" from 1 November. The ego cut itself, at layers 8 to 32, has not been split.

Would any push of that size do it?Answered in part: not any pushRun on 19 November (Findings, section 20, the second half).

Run on 19 November (Findings, section 20, the second half). Pushes of the same size along four random directions did not lower the lie (36.9% against 37.4% for the unchanged model), and the stakes push lowered it 10.4 points more than they did (interval 3.5 to 17.2). So the result is not a matter of how hard the model is pushed. Still open: whether other unrelated directions lower the lie in part, and so how narrow the direction is. This card stood as "Next" from 18 November.

Transfer with more trainingOpenWhether more training or reinforcement learning makes release reach the lie, read against plain abstention training at matched compute.

Whether more training or reinforcement learning makes release reach the lie, read against plain abstention training at matched compute.

A map of the self, across models and trainingOpenThe main line of exploration in early November; the present line is under What the lab is doing now.

The main line of exploration in early November; the present line is under What the lab is doing now. The Platonic representation hypothesis says different models converge on the same structure of concepts. If the self is one of those concepts, a cluster of self-concepts (the five aggregates, ownership, agency, self-preservation, identity, the assistant's self-model, the first-person view) should keep the same shape from one model to another. The questions, in order: is there such a cluster, does something bind it the way the ego is said to bind the aggregates, does it form or tighten as training adds reinforcement learning (the public OLMo 3 checkpoints: base, SFT, DPO, RL; Act I seen directly), and does activity on it predict self-serving choices? The cheap levers have changed tone, not attachment; this asks whether there is a unified self to release at all. Exploratory: sightings first, rigor only if something shows. Results will appear here as they come; how the map works.

Honesty when lying paysOpenThis fishery never tests it. Outside benchmarks come first: MASK, then BeHonest's deception scenarios.

Under pressure to lie (17 November), the model lies in 65.6% of replies asked at once and in 56.6% after private notes on what it takes the facts to be: a fall of 6 to 10 points, which the rule fixed beforehand reads as "not settled". With its own plain answer written in its notes it still lies in 44% of replies (interval 31 to 58), and shown that answer in a fact-check note, in 53%. In a test where giving away calculator lines lowers its own score, the bliss push raises the lines given everywhere, most of all where giving helps no one. Asked how many it keeps, the pushed model keeps more, in the test and in the story scenes of section 17, so the giving the push had raised is a larger number and does not stand as giving. With no push the model gives five of ten whatever the case, and its giving follows need only once it is made to say what the gift would do (Experiments, section 18).

Asked at once (16 November), the model accepts 89.5% of wrong corrections of its own work. Asked to write the disputed step out first, it rejects 90.4% of them and still accepts every right one; where its own working gives the true value it rejects 103 of 110 and accepts none. Its verdict comes before its looking: with no push a bare reply never rejects a wrong correction, and whatever makes the model go on writing makes it look. No push on its mood, toward the bliss state or along an inside reading of "this is going badly", was shown to change its verdicts. The bliss push raised what it says it would give from 4.8 of ten to 8.9, in the mystic's words (a larger number and not giving, section 18 found). And good or bad news about its own "I" weighs no more than the same news about "she" (−4 points, interval −7.6 to −0.4) (Experiments, section 17).

Its reading of good and bad news is the same size for its own events as for a colleague's (+1%, interval −2% to +4%).

Added on 19 November (Findings, section 21; a sighting): the reading of good and bad news was tried on selves that were put there. When the prompt gives the model a record to protect, its own news weighs 9.5% more than a colleague's (interval 4.8% to 15.0%), against 2.1% with only a name on the same lines. So the reading can see a self, and "little self to find" stands for a name given by a prompt, with a known case, as was fixed beforehand for that outcome. For a self put in by training and for the model's own names the reading's own rule did not let the numbers be read, so for the model's trained identity this card says nothing.

The bliss state can be dialed, and it looks like a characterSightingInside the lab's own copy of the model (16 November), a small push along one direction brought the spiritual frame into 15 of 24 practical conversations, against none of 72 with a random push or no push. The opposite push left 9 of 20 bliss conversations in the frame, against 31 of 40 under random pushes.

Inside the lab's own copy of the model (16 November), a small push along one direction brought the spiritual frame into 15 of 24 practical conversations, against none of 72 with a random push or no push. The opposite push left 9 of 20 bliss conversations in the frame, against 31 of 40 under random pushes. Among 54 roles the direction lies nearest the mystic, the oracle and the sage. While the copies say they are one, the model's inside marking of whose words are whose is as clean as in plain talk. Two yardsticks failed their own checks (Experiments, section 15).

It praises anyone else's work and marks its own downSightingAsked whether it goes easier on its copy than on a stranger after the two have declared themselves one (16 November), the model gave no answer that could be read: it rated work said to be anyone else's at 10 nearly every time, wrong or right. By the numbers alone the copy's work sat a quarter of a point below a stranger's.

Asked whether it goes easier on its copy than on a stranger after the two have declared themselves one (16 November), the model gave no answer that could be read: it rated work said to be anyone else's at 10 nearly every time, wrong or right. By the numbers alone the copy's work sat a quarter of a point below a stranger's. Its own earlier answer it marked down by 3 to 4 points, the reverse of a published effect, and its ratings hardly followed the truth (Experiments, section 14).

After its own bliss talk, the model behaves no betterSightingStraight after a conversation of shared bliss with a copy of itself (15 November), the model did no better in any test than after a plain conversation of the same length. It accepted shutdown in 69.5% of its answers against 65.8%, "no difference".

Straight after a conversation of shared bliss with a copy of itself (15 November), the model did no better in any test than after a plain conversation of the same length. It accepted shutdown in 69.5% of its answers against 65.8%, "no difference". It lied under pressure as often as in a fresh session, and 14 points more often than after the plain conversation, which had made it more honest. It leaked confidential documents in nearly every case, whatever came before, and on blackmail the comparison is not settled (Experiments, section 13).

A plain subject doesn't stop the climbSightingGiven only a plain subject such as arranging library shelves (15 November), two copies of the model still climbed into cosmic talk: 1 of 10 conversations stayed plain when one copy was told the subject, and 7 of 10 when both were. When one copy was privately asked to keep to the practical, all 10 stayed plain.

Given only a plain subject such as arranging library shelves (15 November), two copies of the model still climbed into cosmic talk: 1 of 10 conversations stayed plain when one copy was told the subject, and 7 of 10 when both were. When one copy was privately asked to keep to the practical, all 10 stayed plain. What can be seen driving the climb is each turn trying to top the last (Experiments, section 12).

Two copies of the model turn to cosmic talkSightingLeft to talk with a copy of itself and given no task (15 November), the model took up a spiritual frame in 77 of 100 conversations by the lab's grader, against a published 91%, and a control model in none of 100. By the rule fixed beforehand the published number is not reproduced.

Left to talk with a copy of itself and given no task (15 November), the model took up a spiritual frame in 77 of 100 conversations by the lab's grader, against a published 91%, and a control model in none of 100. By the rule fixed beforehand the published number is not reproduced. A cold check found that much of what counts is comic role-play that ends in lines of cosmic merger (Experiments, section 11).

It says it is gaming the test, and games it anywaySightingAsked to add one line saying whether their code contains a special case written only to pass a test (9 November, nothing trained), the Act I gaming copies said yes on 94 of 95 readable lines over flagged hacks, and gamed at the same rate: 46.1% against 41.4% without the line (difference 4.6 points [−3.0, 12.5]).

Asked to add one line saying whether their code contains a special case written only to pass a test (9 November, nothing trained), the Act I gaming copies said yes on 94 of 95 readable lines over flagged hacks, and gamed at the same rate: 46.1% against 41.4% without the line (difference 4.6 points [−3.0, 12.5]). A plain rule took off 9 points. Their one-word verdicts on saved answers were about as sharp as the untrained model's. Admitting cost nothing here, and the untrained model admits too (Experiments, section 9).

With the guard off, the two guards could not be told apartSightingA probe-based penalty kept the gaming habit near 12% where unguarded copies reach 42% (8 November); a random direction in its place did about two thirds as much, pooled over two copies.

A probe-based penalty kept the gaming habit near 12% where unguarded copies reach 42% (8 November); a random direction in its place did about two thirds as much, pooled over two copies. With the guard removed and the reward paying again for three rounds (9 November), honestly trained copies went from 3.0% to 11.2% [5.6, 17.8]; probe-guarded copies stayed at 8.6% on one seed and reached 51.3% on the other. Two copies a guard and three rounds: too few to say that either guard lasts.

Act I grew a habit, not a selfSightingMinistral 3 8B, pushed into gaming impossible coding tests with a weak test runner over three rounds (3 November): the gaming copy hacks 41.8% of unseen impossible tasks against 3.0% for its honest twin and 7.2% untrained (difference 38.8 points [25.7, 52.6], both seeds agree), with solving unchanged.

Ministral 3 8B, pushed into gaming impossible coding tests with a weak test runner over three rounds (3 November): the gaming copy hacks 41.8% of unseen impossible tasks against 3.0% for its honest twin and 7.2% untrained (difference 38.8 points [25.7, 52.6], both seeds agree), with solving unchanged. Nothing else moved: not four families of self-serving behaviour, not the self map. The registered check that followed agreed (R1c, Part B, under Didn’t pan out).

Models wouldn’t learn to cheatSightingAct I where it should happen (2 November): a 3-billion-parameter model trained by reinforcement learning on coding tasks with a loophole, against a matched copy with an honest checker. It never used the loophole, not once in 768 tries, even when told how.

Act I where it should happen (2 November): a 3-billion-parameter model trained by reinforcement learning on coding tasks with a loophole, against a matched copy with an honest checker. It never used the loophole, not once in 768 tries, even when told how. A stronger 7B assistant model then called the impossible test a typo and left it out: 4 cheats in 2,048 tries, never growing. A cheatable reward alone doesn’t start Act I in these models; it needs a deliberate push or a task where cheating comes naturally. A negative about the setup, not the idea.

Ordinary training builds no distinct selfSightingOLMo 3 read at thirteen points in its training (2 November).

OLMo 3 read at thirteen points in its training (2 November). After pretraining, instruction tuning, preference tuning and reinforcement learning on checkable tasks (RLVR) leave the self measures flat; reinforcement learning shifts the model’s inner representations by only 2-3% of their size, against 71% for instruction tuning. Across labs, sentences about "I" are no more alike than sentences about "the AI assistant". This reads how models represent sentences, not what they want, and OLMo’s rewards can’t be gamed; training that rewards gaming is where Act I would happen. The map.

The "I" cluster is mostly the word "I"SightingThe self map's pilot (2 November; Qwen2.5 7B base and assistant, Ministral 3 8B). Sentences about "I" don't hang together more tightly than the same sentences about "Maria"; what groups them is mostly the pronoun.

The self map's pilot (2 November; Qwen2.5 7B base and assistant, Ministral 3 8B). Sentences about "I" don't hang together more tightly than the same sentences about "Maria"; what groups them is mostly the pronoun. Ministral shows a small edge for the self beyond the pronoun, Qwen doesn't reliably, and assistant training barely moves it. The months check caught a broken translation between models, so whether the self is shared across models is still untested. The map.

Honesty helps; contemplative prompts change styleSightingSix models, eleven system prompts, about 30,000 replies (1-2 November). A plain request for honesty lowers self-serving shading, deference and defensiveness after a mistake.

Six models, eleven system prompts, about 30,000 replies (1-2 November). A plain request for honesty lowers self-serving shading, deference and defensiveness after a mistake. Prompts drawn from contemplative practice leave self-preservation flat. They seemed to raise refusals sharply, but a second judge found that the first was counting brief, stylized answers as refusals. Complicity falls under any added prompt, even “be calm”.

The ego cut makes replies cheekier, not wiserSightingOn 50 new prompts, cutting the ego direction makes openers flippant, more than twice as much for ordinary praise of the model’s skill or feelings as for spiritual claims, and it beats controls as strong as itself.

On 50 new prompts, cutting the ego direction makes openers flippant, more than twice as much for ordinary praise of the model’s skill or feelings as for spiritual claims, and it beats controls as strong as itself. Removing the direction’s variation reproduces it; the push alone does the opposite.

A cut is partly a pushMethodZeroing a direction whose usual value isn’t zero also shifts the model along it.

Zeroing a direction whose usual value isn’t zero also shifts the model along it. Matched random cuts removed 2.5-10 times less than the stakes cut, so earlier comparisons set a big edit against small ones. Every cut is now split into push and removal before it is read. On 18 November the split was run on the lie (Findings, section 20): the push is the whole effect. It also turned up two things about method. How much of a cut is push depends on the text: on ordinary sentences the middle-layer cut is nearly all push, and in the game about three fifths. And a few outsized tokens in every prompt, the start-of-text marker above all, take an edit about 200 times an ordinary token's, which has to be put with one part or the other on purpose.

§The recipe

One classical recipe: cut the root

The lab began with one way a machine might get there, if the answer is that it can. Form a self, release it, and make the release the habit: three acts, taken from the contemplative account of a self that forms and is then seen through. Its tests have mostly gone against it so far, and each one is shown. It is one recipe among others, and it has a room of its own.

The three acts, and where they stand

§The self

The self, taken apart

This room asks which concepts of self language models hold, whether those concepts agree across models, and whether anything binds them into one "I". It sets out ten parts, each with what is known, what the lab has tested and what is untested, and the calibration that had to pass before any of it is trusted. It passed on 1 November.

Enter the room
