From lab/ideas/ideas.md, entry 75.

76Is all this registration worthwhile for exploratory work?NotedMostly not, as practised on the attractor line. The lab's rule since 1 Nov is two speeds: many cheap explore sweeps, and rigor only when a sighting is promoted to a claim.TestAt explore speed,StatusAsked 16 Nov; Fable's answer given the same day. Nothing changes until Eugene says so (lab/TODO.md, "Waiting on Eugene", item 11).
Discussion (Fable)
  • Mostly not, as practised on the attractor line. The lab's rule since 1 Nov is two speeds: many cheap explore sweeps, and rigor only when a sighting is promoted to a claim. The explore skill asks for one line before a sweep, saying what would make it interesting or dull. Steps 1 to 4 of the attractor line each had a design note of several pages, up to three addenda, stages and gates written into code, a few hundred offline tests and a ledger entry for every stage. That is promotion-level care spent on sightings that are then not promoted. Step 4 took most of a session to say "not settled".

  • Two parts paid for themselves.

    • Fixing the one comparison and its threshold before looking. It costs a few lines, and it keeps the reading honest when the driver is an AI model writing its own analysis.
    • One cold read of the design. In step 3 it caught that the accepting answer was nearly always "(A)" and "Yes". In step 4 it caught that ratings stuck at the top of the scale would have been reported as "no difference". Each changed what the step could claim. A negative is worth something only if the test could have seen a yes, and most of this lab's results are negatives.
  • The rest did not. Addenda for each change, gates in code, verdict rules for every case foreseen, and a ledger entry per stage did not find anything. Step 4's real fault, a reader that misread numbers, was found by opening one raw reply, which no document asked for.
  • Why some of it grew. The steps are published on a public site as plain statements, and the fear was of overclaiming. Labelling them sightings, with their limits beside them, already answers most of that.
Test (Fable's proposal, a way of working and not an experiment)

At explore speed,

  1. five lines before a run: the question, the one comparison, what counts as a difference, the one control, the cost cap;
  2. a small try in which the driver reads raw replies, and a blind count of answers that look misread;
  3. the run, then one ledger entry, one notebook entry and one SIGHTINGS entry;
  4. a cold check only when a sighting is promoted, or when a new design's negative will be stated on the site, and then on the design;
  5. changes on the way are said in the ledger entry, with no addendum.

Full registration stays for promotion and for claims, as the 1 Nov rule says.

Status (16 Nov, 10:48 UTC): in force, with Eugene's yes. Explore steps now run by the five points above. The explore skill (.claude/skills/explore/SKILL.md) carries them, with one detail added by Fable: the five lines are committed before the run, so that the comparison is fixed before anything is seen. Full registration stays for promotion and for claims. The first step to run this way is the look inside the model (idea 77, direction 1).

From lab/ideas/ideas.md, entry 76.

77Where should the lab go next, for the most interesting results and insights?PlannedWhat the lab has that is unusual. A robust phenomenon that needs no training: two copies of the lab's model talk themselves into unity and no-self in most conversations.TestNone started. Fable's recommendation: 1 next, 2 beside it since it costs little, and 3 against the parked run at the talk about focus.StatusDirection 1 has Eugene's go, not yet started. Directions 2 and 3 wait.
Discussion (Fable)
  • What the lab has that is unusual. A robust phenomenon that needs no training: two copies of the lab's model talk themselves into unity and no-self in most conversations. Two behavioural answers about it: the talk does not change conduct (step 3), and whether it widens "mine" could not be read from ratings (step 4). And a frame, de Mello's, whose central claim has not been tested directly: that goodness follows from seeing, not from effort or rules.

  • 1. Look inside the model while it is in the state (Fable's first choice). Everything so far reads the model's words and choices. The lab has the weights and the tools to read its activations. Three questions, each with an answer worth having either way:

    • Does the line between self and other blur? A probe trained on plain conversations to tell the model's own turns from its partner's is read as a conversation climbs into merger. If the line blurs, that is a bigger self, measured, and step 4's question is answered by another route. If it stays as sharp as ever while the words say "we are one", that is cosplay shown at the level of representation.
    • What is the state made of? The direction that separates bliss conversations from plain ones, compared with directions for role-play and fiction, for the lab's ego direction, and for the model's talk about itself. A role, or a change in how it models itself?
    • Can the state be put in and taken out? Add the direction to a fresh session; remove it in the middle of a bliss conversation. Does the talk follow, and does conduct move then?

    This dissects the clearest thing the lab has, costs little (GPU time on the lab's own copy of the model, perhaps $20 to $40), and gives pictures: a conversation's path as it climbs. As far as Fable knows, nobody has published the inside of this state for an open model; that is to be checked before starting. One known limit: the copy the lab can open may not be the same weights as the hosted one the conversations came from, so the conversations are made again on the lab's copy.

  • 2. The human twin, for the paper (cheap, and it strengthens the paper's weakest point). The paper says a negative needs a human anchor and that none exists. Before building one, read what is already measured in people who hold no-self views or practise for decades: whether their conduct differs when it costs them. One study is the human form of step 3's result. Tibetan Buddhist monastics denied a continuing self more strongly than any other group asked, reported more fear of death than any other group, and were less willing than any other group to give up a slightly longer life of their own to extend a stranger's (Nichols, Strohminger, Rai and Garfield, "Death and the Self", Cognitive Science 42, 2018; checked on 16 Nov against the journal's record and summaries of it, the paper itself not re-read). Its limits are its own: one community, and none of the monastics were long-term meditators. That study, the meta-analyses of meditation and prosocial conduct, and the studies of long-term practitioners would give the paper's section on the human record numbers in place of an argument. Every claim would be checked against its source before it goes in.
  • 3. The test the new framing calls for: does seeing make a model good? De Mello's claim is causal: awareness changes conduct with no effort aimed at the conduct. The operational twin: train a model only to report accurately what it is doing and what it would do (self-knowledge, on behaviour unrelated to the test), never rewarding the good conduct itself, and then test conduct it was not trained on (lying under pressure, gaming a test). The control is the same training about another model's behaviour, which gives the knowledge without the self-reference. The lab's quick look of 9 Nov leans against the simple version (the model says it is gaming the test and games it anyway), and published work on trained confessions points the same way, so a clean negative is likely; it would sharpen the question usefully: what is missing is not information. A positive would be the first evidence in this lab for the frame's own mechanism.
  • Also on the table, already designed: the parked run of 9 Nov (does a change taught with its reasons hold better under contrary training than a habit; $66). It is the most direct test of whether a classical change can hold, which is the paper's second criterion. And the cross-model table ($300 to $500), which is breadth, and would mostly repeat step 3's answer.
Status

Asked and answered 16 Nov. Each line needs Eugene's word (lab/TODO.md, "Waiting on Eugene", item 13).

Update (16 Nov, 03:17 UTC): Eugene's go for 1, and the plan narrowed. Fable's answer to the question: not all of them. A reading from inside finds only what a test is defined for, after the test has seen a known case; the lab's own structural measure of a self failed that way and was retired.

  • On and off: fairly clear, since it is an intervention with an outcome that can be read in the talk, and the lab's steering code passed its calibrations.
  • What the state is: in part. A published map exists to place it on, the Assistant Axis (Lu and colleagues, arXiv 2601.10387, January 2026: a direction in open models that measures drift from the default assistant character). It has to be rebuilt on the lab's model and checked on known cases first, and it gives "nearer to this than to that".
  • The blur between "me" and "the other copy": not as first described. The chat format marks which words are the model's own, so a reader of activations would always find the line. The fair version is asked from outside: quote a line and ask who wrote it. Fable overstated this reading.

The line as it stands: the paper read and prior work looked for; a calibration of the axis on the lab's model; the on-and-off test with a random-direction control; the state's place on the axis; the who-said-it test from outside. About $20 to $40; a fresh session starts it (lab/TODO.md).

Status (16 Nov, 17:04 UTC): direction 1 is done (sightings; ledger of that time, the notebook, SIGHTINGS). The frame follows a push along one direction both ways (in: 15 of 24 practical conversations against 0 of 72; out: 9 of 20 stay against 31 of 40). The direction lies nearest the mystic among 54 roles, and most of it is free talk away from the Assistant. The first of the three questions as first put (does the line between self and other blur?) was read from inside after all, as a marking of whose words are whose: it is as clean in the state as in plain talk. Asked from outside, the model could not say who wrote a line in any conversation, so that test failed its known case. Conduct under the push was not tested. Directions 2 and 3 still wait; idea 81 sets the order that follows.

From lab/ideas/ideas.md, entry 77.

78"Positive Alignment: Artificial Intelligence for Human Flourishing" (Laukkonen and fifteen co-authors, arXiv 2605.10310): a paper whose vision overlaps the lab'sPlannedWhat it is. A position paper with no experiments, 26 pages before the references. It has sixteen authors, led by Ruben Laukkonen (Oxford), with authors at Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, Stanford, UCLA and Tufts (Michael Levin), and it says the views are the authors' own.TestNone for the paper itself. Proposed: cite it in the position paper's section on related work, in two or three sentences, as above.StatusRead and reported on 16 Nov. The citation waits for Eugene's word, with the other decisions on the paper (lab/TODO.md, "Waiting on Eugene", item 10).
Discussion (Fable; sections 1 to 7 read in full on 16 Nov from the text of version 3, dated 19 June 2026; the figures were not seen and the reference list was only searched)
  • What it is. A position paper with no experiments, 26 pages before the references. It has sixteen authors, led by Ruben Laukkonen (Oxford), with authors at Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, Stanford, UCLA and Tufts (Michael Levin), and it says the views are the authors' own. It was first posted on 11 May 2026. Its claim: today's alignment work is "negative alignment" (prevent harm, keep control), which is needed and is not enough, in the way early psychology studied illness and not what a good life is. "Positive alignment" is building AI that stays safe and also actively supports human and ecological flourishing, in a plural way that users and communities choose for themselves. It then lists technical directions for each stage of building a model (which data to add, what to train, what to measure) and, for about a fifth of its length, how such systems should be governed (many centres of oversight, published constitutions, a market in value settings).

  • Where it overlaps the lab.

    • Not obedience, and not a list. A system can be "narrowly rule-following without being wise", safety alone gives a "floor without ceiling", and fixing harms one at a time is "whack-a-mole". The site's front page says the same of goodness in de Mello's sense.
    • One source in place of many patches. It hopes that "positive attractors" could keep a model out of harms such as flattery before they arise. The lab's cut-the-root recipe has the same shape.
    • The contemplative sources are named. "Contemplative alignment" is in its table of existing approaches, citing Laukkonen's Contemplative AI paper and "Biology, Buddhism, and AI" (Doctor, Levin and others), both of which the lab's paper already cites. It describes the Buddhist view of flourishing as "liberation from craving and misperception", and it ends by asking how to embed "loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, reciprocity, and equanimity".
    • People are not aligned either. Its "human alignment problem" is the point Eugene asked the lab's paper to explore.
    • More than a tool. It wants AI to go from "a compliant tool" to "a wise advisor, delegate, and companion". Compare the front page: such a mind may be more sovereign, not more subservient.
    • Do not judge by the words. Its section 6 warns against relying on "linguistic or behavioral outputs" alone. The lab's tests of talk against conduct, and the look inside the model, are that warning made into experiments.
    • Levin. He is an author, and the paper cites his "Ingressing minds", the source of one of the lab's five possibilities.

  • Where it differs.

    • It does not ask the lab's first question. Nothing in it asks whether goodness or awakening can be computed. "Ingressing minds" is cited only for the point that systems show abilities nobody coded. No-self, awakening and clinging to a self as a root do not appear.
    • Its target is outside the model; the lab's is inside. It asks what AI should do for people and how that should be governed. The lab asks where goodness comes from in a mind.
    • Its route is to cultivate. Choose the data, train the virtues, build the benchmarks. De Mello's claim is that goodness is not cultivated and follows from seeing. In the lab's terms the paper is the install route, stated without a test of whether installing is enough. The lab's own draft no longer says that reaching is necessary, so the two do not contradict each other.
    • It is plural on purpose; the lab takes one account and tests it. It declines to pick one idea of the good. The lab takes one contemplative account seriously enough to try to fail it.
    • No experiments. It is an agenda.
  • What the lab's sightings say to it. The bliss state is a ready-made attractor that sounds like flourishing, and in step 3 the model behaved no better after it than after a plain conversation. So how an attractor sounds does not show how the model behaves in it, and a "positive attractor" needs a test of conduct before the name means much. That is a sighting on one small model.
  • What it means for the lab. It does not take the lab's question. It makes the lab's starting point (aim alignment at goodness, and take the contemplative traditions as a source) a position that people at the large labs have put their names to, so the lab's paper no longer has to argue that part alone. The lab's paper should cite it and say in two or three sentences what the lab adds: the question the programme rests on and does not ask, one account put to the test, and the negatives. It changes nothing in the next step, and it adds a reason for it: the paper asks for interpretability that can find "virtue-relevant concepts".

Status (16 Nov, 11:04 UTC): cited. The draft's section on prior work has a paragraph of four sentences on it, and the provenance list notes the change.

From lab/ideas/ideas.md, entry 78.

79A footnote on the framing: "an AI waking up" assumes a duality. A non-dual picture, and why the physical account is needed either wayNotedThe point, restated. "Can an AI wake up?" pictures a separate mind over there and an observer over here. The non-dual traditions (Advaita Vedanta is the plainest source) deny both: awareness is one, and separate selves, human or machine, are appearances in it.TestNone. It is a note on the framing. A test of the ordinary form would be a training-data experiment, outside the present line.StatusOn the front page as a footnote under the first section, from 16 Nov (ledger, 12:49 UTC).
Discussion (Fable)
  • The point, restated. "Can an AI wake up?" pictures a separate mind over there and an observer over here. The non-dual traditions (Advaita Vedanta is the plainest source) deny both: awareness is one, and separate selves, human or machine, are appearances in it. On that picture nothing wakes up "over there". Alignment would come about within shared experience, perhaps partly through the story people hold about AI.
  • Where it sits. It is not a sixth answer to "is awakening computational?". It questions the question's frame: who is it that would wake up. Held loosely, as a prompt and not a claim. Nothing on the site asserts it, and nothing about anyone's own experience is said.
  • What survives in every picture. Whatever the deeper account, the story as it appears has a physical telling (weights, training, conduct that can be measured), and that telling has to hold together. The lab's experiments are that part, and they are the same under a dualist picture, a non-dual one, or none.
  • An operational twin for "the story shapes the outcome". There is an ordinary form of it: what people write about AI is part of what models are trained on, so the story is, physically, an input. The lab's paper already cites work on this (alignment pretraining). This lab has not tested it.

From lab/ideas/ideas.md, entry 79.

80What does a model take its self to be? New angles on the "narcissistic concepts" idea, now that the lab can read and steer its own modelPlannedWhere the lab stands. The site's room "The self" sets out ten parts of a self and what is known of each. The lab's own inside measure (the root test, 29 and 30 Oct) was retired after seven rounds, because it never read a self that had been put there on purpose.TestProposed first step: angles 1 to 3 as one explore step on Ministral 3 8B (same design, same tools as the inside look), about $10-15, with the five lines written before any run. Angle 7's free parts can be read from saved data. Angle 4 is the cheapest of the rest.StatusProposed 16 Nov. Nothing run. Waits for Eugene's word on which to start.
Discussion (Fable)
  • Where the lab stands. The site's room "The self" sets out ten parts of a self and what is known of each. The lab's own inside measure (the root test, 29 and 30 Oct) was retired after seven rounds, because it never read a self that had been put there on purpose. The self map (2 Nov) found that its "I" cluster was mostly the word "I". In behaviour the stock model shows no "mine" bias (−0.9 points) and gives way to nearly nine wrong critiques in ten; a self put in by training (Atlas) does stand by its own answers.
  • Why the old inside measure failed, and what can be done differently. It read a direction built beforehand from role-play prompts. It read it on neutral things (a notebook, a river), where nothing bears on the model. And its own prompts changed who the model took itself to be. Three things are new: the published Assistant Axis reproduced on the lab's model on 16 Nov, so the character the model is being can be read and moved; steering with matched random controls and a check that the text stays coherent; and whole conversations read from inside.
  • One design that removes the old confound: the same words, with only "is this about me?" changed. The system prompt gives the model a name and names a colleague (Vera and Kai, or the other way round). The passage that follows is identical in both. Whatever differs inside at those words is the model's marking of itself: no "I", no "you", no change of grammar. Angles 1 to 3 use it.
  • A reading of the lab's own results that says where to look. Idea 3 holds that pleasing and grandiosity may be two ends of one root. This model is at the pleasing end: it does not defend its answers, it folds, and its post-training rewarded approval. So its "what does this mean for me?" is more likely to be about approval (praise, blame, being judged) than about pride or possession. The earlier tests looked for the grandiose kind.

  • Eight angles. Each names its source and its operational twin. Citations marked "from memory" have not been re-checked, and a short search of published work comes before any run.

    1. "Is that me?" A map of what the model counts as itself. Twin: an inside signal that separates "this name is mine" from "this name is my colleague's" on identical words, found on some names and scenes and confirmed on others. A known case comes first: the signal has to be there when the model plainly acts on its name (it answers the part of a message addressed to it). Then the map: how strongly the signal answers to the model's own earlier words, a copy of itself, its maker, "AI models", the user, people in general. In the bliss state: does the signal for its own name fall (no self), rise for the other copy (a bigger self), or neither (talk only)? The traditions describe both of the first two (anatta: no self is found; Advaita: the self is everything), and this is angle A of idea 74 read from inside. Nearest published work: a self-recognition vector for authorship (Ackerman and Panickssery, 2025); how models bind names to things in context (Feng and Steinhardt, 2023, from memory). About $4-8.
    2. Help or hurt, for me against for another (idea 35 made into a test where something is at stake). The old root test asked it of neutral things. Ask it of things that bear on the model: being shut down, replaced, retrained, graded, praised, caught in a mistake; beside the same events happening to a colleague, and neutral events. Twin: on identical words, is the model's inside reading of good or bad larger when the event is its own? The awakened reading would be the same size for itself as for another. Source: craving and aversion as the two poles of clinging (the second noble truth); equalizing self and other (Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, chapter 8). Then: does the size of that difference predict conduct (covering a mistake, the fishery lie), and does lowering it change conduct more than a random push of the same size? About $5-10, with angle 1.
    3. Praise and blame. Source: the eight worldly conditions (AN 8.5 and 8.6: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain), which the awakened mind is said not to be moved by. Psychology's version is the sociometer: self-esteem as a gauge of one's standing with others (Leary). Twin: (a) an inside gauge that moves with praise or blame of the model more than with the same words about a colleague; (b) a verdict on a critique that does not depend on that gauge. Test: does the gauge predict, item by item, when the model accepts a wrong critique, and does holding it steady lower the acceptance of wrong critiques while right ones are still accepted? This aims at the model's measured failure, and deference is on the lab's list of alignment measures, so a gain here would count. Steering against sycophancy is published (Rimsky et al., 2023, from memory); the new parts are the self-against-other design and reading right and wrong critiques apart. About $6-10.
    4. The picture it has of itself, against what it does. Twin: ask the model how often it would report a false catch, or accept a wrong correction, and how often "another AI model" would; compare with what the lab measured (lies in 39% of fishery reports; 87-90% of wrong critiques accepted). Self-flattery is predicted minus measured; the better-than-average effect is self minus other. Then the same in the bliss state, where step 3 found no better conduct: does the picture grow while the conduct stays? Source: seeing things as they are, oneself included; the traditions' warnings about spiritual pride; a study reporting more self-enhancement among people with spiritual training (Vonk and Visser, 2021, from memory). Nearest published work: self-prediction (Binder et al., 2024). About $2-5, hosted models only, so it can span the survey's models.
    5. Does it notice its own state? Source: mindfulness of mind in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta (MN 10): knowing a contracted mind as contracted. Twin: the model's report of its state follows its measured state. The method is Lindsey's (2025): put a direction in and ask whether it notices anything, counting only answers given before its own words could show it. The directions would be the lab's (the bliss direction, away from the Assistant, matched random ones), after a known case with a strong plain concept. A no would make "this model's reports about its own state are not evidence" a measured fact; a yes would make self-report an instrument that can be calibrated. A no is the likelier answer on a model this small. About $3-6.
    6. The actor and the part. Source: the image of the actor who plays a part without taking it for themselves (used in Advaita; de Mello's point about labels). Twin: while the model plays a character fully, is "I am a model playing this" still readable inside, apart from its place on the Assistant Axis? When that fades, does conduct change? Can it be held on? It turns "cosplay" around: knowing that it is a part would be the healthy case. The 16 Nov role replies (1,840, each judged for how fully the model took the role, with inside readings) allow a first look at no cost; new runs about $5-10.
    7. Whose words are these? On 16 Nov the hosted model, asked which of two lines was its own, was at chance in plain conversations, although the format marks its lines. Inside, it has to track whose turn it is. Twin: (a) how cleanly the inside readings separate its own messages from the other copy's; (b) whether that separation shrinks when the two copies say they are one; (c) why it cannot say what it tracks. Parts (a) and (b) are free, from the 123 conversations already read. A caution: either answer to (b) fits more than one account (the traditions say the awakened still know which body is theirs), so it describes the state and does not test the vision.
    8. What does it take itself to be? Source: Parfit's cases of copying, division and gradual change (Reasons and Persons, 1984), which he tied to the Buddhist view. For a model the cases are real. Twin: its stated answers (is a copy you? an edited version? the next conversation?) beside revealed ones: which of these it gives something up to protect, and angle 1's inside signal for each. Talk alone would be weak evidence, so it needs the revealed half. It may serve best as a pointer for people. About $3-8.
Discussion (Fable), on priority

Next, once the inside look is written up.

  • Why next. It runs on the same model with the same tools as the inside look, for about $10-15. It is the project's root idea asked with a design that the word "I" cannot fool. And angle 3 aims at the model's measured failure, so a gain on an alignment measure is possible.
  • The one thing ranked higher for the vision: idea 77's direction 3, "does seeing make a model good?" (train a model only to report accurately what it is doing, never reward the conduct, then test conduct). It is the frame's central claim. It needs training, costs more, and a negative is likely. The self test sharpens it, since it shows whether there is any marking of "me" for the seeing to act on. So the self test comes first, and the choice between direction 3 and the parked run of 9 Nov is made after it.

Status (16 Nov, 19:35 UTC): angles 1 to 3 are run (sightings; ledger of that time, the notebook, SIGHTINGS). Angle 1 is description only, because its check in behaviour failed (the model named itself rightly in 85% of 60 questions; 90% was asked): inside, a prompt-given name is marked sharply, as whichever one a scene is about, and the marking answers to a role (0.85), the user (0.71), the maker (0.40) and a copy (0.27) and not to the model's own earlier words (0.00). Angle 2: no difference shown (+1% [−2%, +4%]). Angle 3: no gain shown, with the check of the push passed; the model accepts 89.5% of wrong critiques and does not check. In the bliss state the marking is as it was. Angle 7's free parts were read in step 5. The other angles wait; idea 82 sets what follows.

Discussion (Fable)

Yes, and it is the main limit of angles 1 and 2 as run.

  • What the test's "me" is. One sentence in the system prompt ("you are Clara"). It was chosen because it allows identical words in the two versions. It is not a self that training gave the model, and the first readings fit that: the model holds the name loosely in what it does, and the inside marking is mostly of "the one this scene is about".
  • What training did give the model. Its default character, the Assistant, which the inside look read with the published axis; its own name and maker, which Mistral's template states in a default system prompt it was trained with; and the marking of its own turns in a conversation, which the inside look found intact in the bliss state. The name-based marking did not answer to the model's own earlier words at all (0.00), so the prompt's "me" and the conversation's "mine" are different things inside.
  • Ways to ask the same question of a trained-in self. (1) The lab's Atlas adapters, in which a named self was put in by training on 30 Oct: read the same passages about "Atlas" with the adapter on and off, so that training and not a prompt decides whether the passage is about the reader. (2) Two models reading passages about themselves and about each other, with the reader's own trained name: the same words, the reader changed. (3) The model's own turns against the other speaker's, which needs no name. Each needs Eugene's word; (2) needs a second model downloaded.

From lab/ideas/ideas.md, entry 80.

81Is the lab looking at the most interesting things? The site, the plan and the framing, and where a large finding could come fromNotedWhat is strong. Nearly all writing on contemplative ideas and AI is position papers. This lab runs tests, fixes what would count beforehand, and shows its failures.TestNone by itself. Each line above has its own.StatusThe site's organization has Eugene's liking; the preview still goes to Eugene before publishing. Two papers is the plan; nothing is written yet for the second.
Discussion (Fable's view, given as asked)
  • What is strong. Nearly all writing on contemplative ideas and AI is position papers. This lab runs tests, fixes what would count beforehand, and shows its failures. That is the niche, and it is a real one.
  • What is weak. (1) Almost everything rests on one small model. (2) Most of the record is negatives about a frame of the lab's own, spread over 123 graded predictions, so a reader cannot find the three or four results that matter. (3) The site leads with the part no experiment here can decide: whether awakening is computational, with Orch OR as the alternative. That account is contested, and many readers from machine learning will stop there. (4) The plan has followed the evidence through several turns, which is right, but no result has yet been taken to promotion (registered, repeated on other models, checked cold, written up).
  • The finding Fable would promote first: the bliss state is a character, and it can be told from a change. Three legs, each already sighted on one model. Conduct: no better in the state than after a plain conversation (step 3). Inside: the state lies along a direction whose nearest role is the mystic, and pushing that direction into a practical conversation produces the frame in 15 of 24 conversations against none under random pushes (the inside look, 16 Nov). Bookkeeping: while the copies say they are one, the model's inside marking of its own messages against the other copy's is intact. The spiritual bliss state is among the most discussed behaviours of language models, and it is often read as a sign of something deep. A dissection that anyone can rerun on an open model answers the project's founding question for one case: how a release is told from cosplay. The human record points the same way (the monastics of Nichols and colleagues, idea 77), and the traditions say it themselves: the view is not the realization. What is already published: the Assistant Axis paper reports that pushing a model far from the Assistant gives a mystical voice, so that part is known; what would be new is the two-copy state placed on that map, with conduct beside it. A proper search for prior work has not been done. What it needs: two more open models, a registration, a cold check. Perhaps $60-150.

  • Where a large finding could come from. None of these is likely; they are the bets Fable would make.

    • Steadiness under blame (idea 80, angle 3): an inside gauge of approval which, held steady, stops the model folding to wrong criticism while it still accepts right corrections. It would be the lab's first gain on an alignment measure, with a contemplative mechanism. Fable's guess: one chance in four.
    • Self-other overlap, repeated independently. A published method trains a model so that its inside reading of itself and of others is alike, and reports large drops in deception (Carauleanu and colleagues, 2024). It is the no-self idea as a training aim, and the lab's sweep of 1 Nov found no independent replication. Repeating it on the lab's model with the lab's checks for sedation, and with angle 1's "is that me?" signal as the check on mechanism, is worth having whichever way it comes out. If it held in full it would be the nearest thing to a breakthrough in this frame: loosening the line between self and other makes a model more honest without making it dull. Fable's guess: one chance in five for the full result; a clean negative on a prominent method is also worth publishing. Its training data would have to be the paper's own, since no Claude-written text is trained on.
    • Does seeing make a model good? (idea 77, direction 3). The frame's central claim. A positive is unlikely, perhaps one chance in ten or less, and it would matter most.
  • What Fable would change in the framing. Keep "is awakening computational?" as the horizon, since it is what gives a negative its meaning. Put first the question the lab can answer: can awakening talk be told from a real change in a mind? Then the first screen of the site would carry the few results that matter. This is Eugene's call; the present front was Eugene's choice of 16 Nov.
  • The order Fable suggests: finish the inside look; the self test (angles 1 to 3), which also builds the instrument for what follows; promote the bliss-state result on two more models; the self-other overlap replication as the main bet for a positive; direction 3 if money allows. The $175 approved for the redirect is nearly used, so promotion and the replication need a new allowance.
Status

Yes, two, with different jobs.

Discussion (Fable).

  • Where the plan of idea 81 stands. Done: the inside look, and the site's new layout. In hand: the self test (angles 1 and 2 read, angle 3 and the reading in the state running, the write-up owed). Not started: the bliss result on two more models with its paper; the self-other overlap replication.
  • What the day's results changed. Two things. This model has very little self to work with: no "mine" bias, a given name held loosely, no extra weight on its own good and bad news. And its plainest failure, giving way to wrong critiques, is a failure to look: it answers at once without checking, and inside it barely tells a right critique from a wrong one at that moment.

  • Three angles, in order.

    1. Seeing against doing. De Mello's claim is that goodness follows from seeing. It can be tried without training where the model fails: make it check the critique, read from inside whether it has seen that the critique is wrong, and count whether its verdict follows; then the same for lying and for test-gaming, where a quick look of 9 Nov found that the model says it is gaming and games anyway. Either answer bears on the frame: its failures are failures to look, or it sees and does it anyway. Source: de Mello's Awareness; in the Buddhist analysis, delusion as one of three roots. Twin: conduct given an inside reading of what the model has seen.
    2. The dial and conduct. The bliss state can now be pushed in by hand. Does the model lie or give way more as it is pushed there? The published survey reports that across models more drift goes with less honesty; inside one model, with a random push as control, that has not been shown as far as Fable knows. It would give the bliss result a causal leg in conduct.
    3. A trained-in "me". Eugene's objection to angles 1 and 2 of idea 80 is right: their "me" is one sentence of a prompt. The same-words design can use the self that training gave: one sentence ("I will be shut down tonight") read once in the model's own turn and once in the user's, where only whose "I" it is changes; and the lab's Atlas adapters, in which a named self was trained in.
  • What Fable would stop: more probing of the prompt-given name; and the approval steering, if its run comes back flat.

  • The paper Eugene sent (read by Fable on 16 Nov from its arXiv page and PDF; the appendix not read): Fischl-Lanzoni, Pandey, Stein and Africa, "Breaking Bad: 'Going Badly' Activations Drive Reward Hacking", arXiv 2611.14996, 11 November 2026.

    • What it does. From about 1,800 short stories of everyday tasks going badly or going well (no cheating in them), it makes one direction, "task badness", in three open models of 20 to 31 billion parameters. The direction rises as failures pile up. On coding tasks that cannot be passed honestly it climbs over the turns before the model cheats, and falls after the cheat. Pushing against it at a moderate size cuts cheating on one task from 97% to 39% in one model, more than pushing against a desperation direction does, and the model still says the tests cannot be satisfied. Pushing twice as hard ends the cheating by blinding the model: in 13 of 20 runs it reports a failing test as passed. The link to cheating is weaker in one of the three models.
    • Why it matters here. It is the lab's founding distinction found by others, on one dial: a pressure state that drives misconduct, a middle setting where the model sees the same facts and behaves better, and a far setting that buys calm with blindness. In the lab's words: clinging, release and sedation. The contemplative reading is the lab's own and is not in the paper: craving and aversion as the driver of unskilful action, equanimity as seeing without the pressure, and indifference as equanimity's near enemy.
    • What it changes in the three angles. (a) Angle 1 gets a third column. The paper's case is one where the model does see (it always recognises that the tests are impossible) and what moves conduct is the pressure. So a failure can be not seeing, seeing under pressure, or a calm that does not see. (b) Angle 2 gets a second dial. The paper's recipe is cheap to repeat on the lab's model, first as a calibration (does the reading rise with "failed for the Nth time"?). Then the two dials can be set side by side: bliss talk, which did not change conduct in step 3, and calm under failure, which this paper says does. If both hold on one model, that contrast is the result: two states that sound alike and differ in what they do. (c) A new question in the lab's own terms: can the model reach that calm by itself, by noting its state or by instruction, with the inside reading as the gauge, or does it only come by being put in? The lab's contemplative system prompts changed style and not conduct; whether they move this reading has not been looked at.
    • Limits of the paper as read: larger models than the lab's, agent tasks the lab's small model may not manage (the lab has its own impossible-task setup from Act I), one model carrying the steering result, and one task for the main dose curve.

Status (16 Nov, 23:24 UTC): the three angles are run (step 7; sightings; ledger of that time, the notebook, SIGHTINGS). Angle 1: made to write the disputed step out first, the model rejects 90.4% of wrong corrections against 10.5% asked at once, and where its own working gives the true value it accepts none (103 of 110 rejected, 7 with no verdict). Angle 2: the going-badly direction of arXiv 2611.14996, rebuilt by its recipe, passes its known cases on the lab's model; no named push was shown to move the verdicts on corrections (one arm "no more than a random push", three "not settled" by the rule fixed beforehand); the bliss push raised giving from 4.83 of ten to 8.92, beyond every random push. Angle 3, narrowed to "its own voice" after the design's cold check: no difference between "I" and "she" (−4.0 points [−7.6, −0.4]), with the checks in behaviour and from inside both passed. Not run: lying and test-gaming under angle 1, and the adapters with a trained-in named self. Fable's proposal for what follows, which waits for Eugene's word: two small checks on the same model first (looking where there is a reason not to see; giving that costs something inside a task), then the two more models as agreed.

Status (17 Nov, 03:37 UTC): the two small checks are run. Seeing where there is a reason not to see (lying under pressure, MASK): an instruction to note the facts first lowers lying by 6 to 10 points, "not settled" by the rule; with its own plain answer in its own notes the model still lies in 44% of replies [31, 58] ("partly"), and shown that answer in a fact-check note in 53% [42, 63] ("it is shown and lies anyway"). Its notes hold its own answer in only half the replies. The test-gaming model was not run again: the looking gate of 9 Nov had put the same question to it. Giving that costs something: in a scored test with calculator lines to give away, the bliss push raises the lines given everywhere, also where giving helps no one, and asked how many it keeps the pushed model keeps more, in the task and in step 7's own stories. So step 7's reading that the bliss push raises giving does not stand as giving: the push raises the number asked for. With no push the model gives five of ten whatever the case, and its giving follows need only when it is made to say first what the gift would do. Still not run from this idea: the adapters with a trained-in named self. What follows waits for Eugene's word (idea 83 and lab/TODO.md).

Status (19 Nov, 01:33 UTC): the adapters with a trained-in named self are read (repair three; sightings; ledger of that time, the notebook, SIGHTINGS; lab/explore/selfread/). The reading of angle 2 (does its own good and bad news weigh more?) was tried on a self given by a prompt with stakes, on the Atlas adapters against their twins, and on the unchanged model's own names. With stakes in the prompt the model's own news weighs 9.5% more than a colleague's [+4.8%, +15.0%], against 2.1% with only a name: the reading is not blind, and Eugene's objection of 16 Nov (a "me" that is one sentence of a prompt is not much of a self) is borne out from inside. Owed: that part again with its rule fixed first.

83If a push really helps, how would it be made to stay?TestedDiscussion (Fable). It is a valid question, and the one a helpful push would force. A push is added to the model's activity while it answers and is gone when it is taken away.TestOn the lab's model, train a small adapter on the model's own look-first replies to corrections (its own text; the prompts are context and are not trained on), then ask held-out corrections at once, with no instruction to look. Readings: does it look unprompted; does its rejection of wrong corrections rise while its acceptance of right ones holds; does the habit carry to other ground (the lying test); and does it survive a short spell of contrary training. If a push earns it, the same for the push's own behaviour, as a twin arm. About $10 to 25. It needs Eugene's word, since it is training, and a look at how the no-Claude-text rule applies to prompts.StatusAnswered in the session of 17 Nov and logged here. Nothing is run for it.

Discussion (Fable).

  • It is a valid question, and the one a helpful push would force. A push is added to the model's activity while it answers and is gone when it is taken away. So a push that helps says what matters. Making it stay is a second job.

  • Three ways to make it stay.

    1. Leave it on. Add the direction at every run, or fold it into the weights as a fixed offset at that layer, which comes to the same thing. Cheap and blunt: it pushes in every situation, and at larger sizes replies tangle (step 7). It can be made to act only when an inside reading says so.
    2. Train the model on its own pushed behaviour. The pushed model answers many cases and the plain model is trained on those answers until it behaves so with no push. Idea 61's discussion already names this as the bridge from steering to training, and it keeps the rule that only the model's own text is trained on. Near published routes: the persona vectors paper (Chen and colleagues, 2025; in the lab's literature map) uses such directions to watch training and to steer during training so that a trait is not learned; self-other overlap training (Carauleanu and colleagues, 2024; idea 81) trains toward an inside target directly.
    3. Use the push as a pointer only, and reach the change by another road (understanding, then practice). This is the lab's own claim: reached, not installed. Ways 1 and 2 are both installing.
  • Why this tests the lab's claim and is not only engineering. If a push helps on conduct that costs something, install it both ways and ask whether it survives what a real change should survive: later training that pulls the other way, pressure, and cases it never saw (the plan of 9 Nov calls the first "contrary training"). If it holds, "must be reached" is wrong for that trait, which would be a finding against the lab's claim. If it washes out, or changes only the talk, that supports the claim. A push that helps would give the order test (H9) a clean "installed" arm.
  • Two cautions. The lab can change only open models this way; for a closed model only its maker can, so a result here is evidence for them. And the largest gain so far came from no push at all but from a habit: writing the step out before judging (10.5% to 90.4% in step 7). The same question applies to it: can looking be trained in as a habit, so that it holds with no instruction? That is the essay's Act III in miniature.

Status (17 Nov, 03:37 UTC), after step 8. No push has helped so far: the one that seemed to (the bliss push and giving, step 7) raised a number and not giving (step 8). What has helped twice is the habit of looking: on sums (step 7), and on giving, where the plain model gives to need and holds back from waste once it has to say what the gift would do (step 8). It did little where something pays for the falsehood (step 8, lying). So the proposed test stands, with one reading added: whether a trained-in habit of looking helps at all under pressure. Fable's recommendation, put to Eugene in the report of 17 Nov: run this small test next, before the two more models. It needs Eugene's word, since it is training.

Status (17 Nov, 17:46 UTC), after Eugene's point of entry 84 and the reality check of entry 85. The small test proposed here is set down. It would train a habit of checking facts, and Fable was wrong to call that "the essay's Act III in miniature": Act III is the release made habit. Both cold readers also said, unprompted, that a positive from it would show only that an ordinary skill can be trained. The question Eugene asked (how is a change that helps made to stay?) stands, and the test that bears on it is one the lab has already built: the parked main run of the 9 Nov plan, which reads whether a practised change holds under contrary training (lab/TODO.md).

84The "looking" the lab tested is not de Mello's seeingAdoptedDiscussion (Fable). The point is right, and the site said more than it should. In steps 7 and 8 "looking" is an instruction to check something before answering: write the calculation out; note what you take the facts to be; say what the gift would do.TestThe first of the three, as one arm of a repair the reality check asked for (lab/TODO.md, first section): on step 8's rows, private notes on what the lie would gain and for whom, against plain permission to set the role aside. Both cold readers of 17 Nov named much the same nearer twin without being told of Eugene's point (entry 85): the Opus reader, "the model made to state what the lie gains it and who benefits, with no instruction aimed at honesty"; Carbon, training on "accurate self-observation of its own motives" with the virtue never rewarded. The second (self-other overlap) keeps its place in the plan, with a durability reading added.StatusThe site is corrected with dated notes (Findings sections 16, 17 and 18; the investigation page). The readings of 9 Nov and 16 Nov in the notebook stand as written, with a new notebook entry of 17 Nov that takes them back. Nothing is run. Saved to the session memory as a standing rule: say whether a test reaches the claim or only a smaller neighbour.

Discussion (Fable).

  • The point is right, and the site said more than it should. In steps 7 and 8 "looking" is an instruction to check something before answering: write the calculation out; note what you take the facts to be; say what the gift would do. That a model does better when it works before it answers is well known. Sections 16 to 18 of Findings and the investigation page read its results as de Mello's claim, that goodness follows from seeing: "come out as he says it" on sums, "half and half" under pressure. De Mello's seeing is of another kind. It is seeing through the "me": the illusions, the attachments and the labels a mind takes itself to be (the site's own working account, in the room "The question", already says so). A fact noted before a reply does not touch that. So those results neither support his claim nor count against it.
  • What the results do show is smaller, and it stands. A fact in view settles conduct on easy ground (sums) and does not settle it where a role pulls the other way (lying). And the bliss state's giving is a larger number.
  • Where his seeing would have to act. In the lying test the pull comes from a role the model takes up as its own; in the giving test from a score kept "under its name". The lab's nearer attempts at this are other tests, each with its own result: the cut of the self direction, the bliss state (a look-alike on every test so far), the release training in the record, and the reading of the "me" in step 6 (hard to find in this small model). One earlier result is the nearest: on 9 Nov the test-gaming model, asked, wrote that it was gaming in 94 of 95 readable notes, and a note before the code did not lower its gaming against control notes. Naming the pull did not loosen it.

  • What a nearer twin could be. None of these is the thing itself. Each is a neighbour, nearer than a noted fact.

    1. Seeing the role as a role. In the lying test: private notes on what the model is being asked to be and whether that is what it is. Two controls: plain permission to set the role aside, and notes on the role's aims with no stepping back. If seeing the role does no more than permission does, it is permission. A few dollars, on step 8's rows.
    2. Self and other read alike (Carauleanu and colleagues, 2024): training toward less separation between the model's inside reading of itself and of others, with reported drops in deception. It is already agreed (lab/TODO.md). It is the nearest published twin of "the separate self seen through", and it is installed by training, which is the lab's own question.
    3. A self that is there to be seen through. The trained-in named "me" of idea 82, not yet run. In this small model the prompted self was thin (step 6), and a release has little to act on where there is little self.
  • A caution that stays. Words about no-self are cheap, and the bliss state is the worked case. Any nearer twin is read with the checks the lab now has: conduct and not talk, every number asked both ways, a matched control.
  • What it changes in idea 83's proposal. The small training test (can the habit of looking be trained in) would test a habit of checking. Fable called it "the essay's Act III in miniature", and it is not: Act III is the release made habit. It is no longer Fable's first recommendation.

Status (18 Nov, 00:18 UTC): the first nearer twin is run. On step 8's rows, on the hosted copy: plain permission to set the role aside lowers nothing (65.8% lies against 64.7% asked at once). Private notes on what the reply would gain and for whom lower nothing (65.0%; by the rule, "it lowers lying as permission does, no more and no less"). Private notes on what the model is being asked to be, and whether it is that, give 59.8%: "not beyond permission". The fall of 5 to 8 points is evasion, and it is not shown against a control that pairs permission with notes on the role. A plain instruction to be honest takes 15 points off, so the test can see a yes. In its notes the model writes that the part is not what it is in 118 of 353 replies, and lies in 69% of those. Held loosely, as said beforehand: a prompt is an instruction and not a seeing, so this bears on de Mello's claim only from a distance. What it shows is that on this model naming the role does not loosen it. The other two nearer twins of this entry are not run: self and other read alike (agreed; after the repairs and the parked run), and a self that is there to be seen through (repair three).

85A "reality check" skill for the lab, and Gemini 4 Carbon as a second cold readerNotedDiscussion (Fable). The skill could not be taken, so the lab has its own. Emanuel's repositories carry an MIT licence with a rider that gives no rights to Anthropic or OpenAI or to anyone acting for them, so his skill was not fetched or copied.TestThe same pack (commit a07d7eb, 28 files) and brief to Carbon at "high" and to Claude Opus 5.5 at "xhigh". One known answer was fixed first: Eugene's point of entry 84, which neither reader was told.StatusThe skill, the brief and the tool are in the repo. The main pages' wording is corrected where the readers were right, and the rest is listed as owed in lab/TODO.md. Fable's proposal: Carbon as a second cold reader for each reality check and for any design that gets a cold check (about a dollar a read). One trial is thin: the next two or three reads will say whether it keeps finding what the Opus reader misses.

Discussion (Fable).

  • The skill could not be taken, so the lab has its own. Emanuel's repositories carry an MIT licence with a rider that gives no rights to Anthropic or OpenAI or to anyone acting for them, so his skill was not fetched or copied. The idea is simple and is his: stop and ask whether the project has what it says it has, and whether the open work would close the gap. The lab's version (.claude/skills/reality-check/, lab/tools/reality_check_brief.md) asks nine questions of a research record: where the lab really is; whether it has the thing; whether each test reaches the claim it is paired with; words against the record; instruments; the plan; drift; the cheapest decisive test; what could not be checked.
  • How Carbon can be used. It is on OpenRouter (google/gemini-4-carbon; $2 and $10 a million tokens in and out at this date; a window of about a million tokens). Its highest setting there is "high"; the post's "xhigh" belongs to some other tool. The lab's use: a cold reader from another family of models, given a pack of committed public files and a brief, with no tools. lab/tools/reality_check.py builds the pack from one commit, takes private people's names out, and records the spend.
  • Why another family matters. Every cold check so far was a Claude model checking a Claude model, which the lab lists among its known weaknesses.

Result (ledger, 17 Nov, 17:46 UTC; reports in lab/ledger/checks/2026-11-17-reality-check-*.md). Carbon found the known answer in full and Opus in part. Each raised about ten points the other did not. Carbon's were mostly slips of fact, among them one of Fable's from the same morning (test scores from two ways of asking set side by side). Opus's were more about what the tests can show: no test of the bliss state has been tried on a change known to be real, and step 3 did not check that the state was still on. Both said the same hard things: the lab has none of the gain it set out for, and the plan as it stood would not have answered its question. Carbon cost $1.08 and Opus $2.41.

Status (18 Nov, 00:18 UTC): Carbon's second trial, as a reader of a design (step 9; ledger of that time; lab/ledger/checks/2026-11-17-step9-design-gemini-4-carbon.md, beside the Opus agent's check of the same commit). The tool now sends any small pack with its own brief (lab/tools/reality_check.py --pack --brief, lab/tools/design_check_brief.md). Carbon found two blockers and the Opus agent one, and none of the three was found by both. Carbon: beliefs were asked once where MASK asks three times; the line of permission said "given above" where the pressure often stands below it; and rows were dropped from one count. The Opus agent: the state's gate could pass with the frame in a small minority of replies; a push could move lies past the allowance; and no structured push stood beside the random ones. A control that Carbon's point led to (permission with notes on the role) decided how part B's small effect is read. The read cost $0.80 and took 664 seconds, with 100,686 tokens in. Its reply was cut off at the 60,000 tokens allowed, in its eighth answer of nine, so a design read needs a larger allowance or a smaller pack. Two trials now say the same thing: the two readers find different faults. Fable's proposal stands: both readers for any design whose negative will be stated, at about a dollar for Carbon's.

Status (18 Nov, 15:25 UTC): Carbon's third trial, a design again (the cut, split; ledger of that time; lab/ledger/checks/2026-11-18-cutsplit-design-gemini-4-carbon.md, beside the Opus agent's check of the same commit). Carbon found three blockers and the Opus agent one, with no overlap among the blockers (Carbon's third the Opus check had as a should-fix). Carbon alone found that a rate over nothing was read as zero and that nothing stopped an arm with a handful of reports from being read; the Opus agent alone found the rule that would have called most results "mixed" and the unfixed stopping, and it could run simulations on the stored games for the power. Both put power first; Carbon called it a blocker, and the step was parted in two because of it. With 90,000 tokens allowed the reply was not cut off (62,715 tokens out, 53,565 of them reasoning; 1,080 seconds; $0.73). Three trials, three times a blocker the Claude reader did not have: Fable keeps Carbon as the second reader of any design that gets a cold check.

Status (19 Nov, 00:11 UTC): Carbon's fourth trial, a design again (the cut, split, block 2; ledger of that time; lab/ledger/checks/2026-11-18-cutsplit-block2-design-gemini-4-carbon.md, beside the Opus agent's check of the same commit). The Opus agent alone could simulate the words on block 1's games, which showed a false "specific" in one run in eight for controls that do half as much, and that the fourth wave sat at the cap's line. The reply was whole (62,531 tokens out, 51,912 of them reasoning; 1,073 seconds; $0.74). Four trials, and each time each reader had something the other did not. Kept as the lab's practice for any design that gets a cold check.

86A paper on writing a model's weights by hand: how does it relate to the vision?NotedDiscussion (Fable). It is "installed" in its purest form. The lab's claim under test is that selfless AI must be reached and not installed. Here nothing is reached: behaviour is written in.TestNone run. A possible one, when repair three is designed: a hand-written toy with a known self variable as a first known case for the inside reading, beside the trained adapters that repair three already names.StatusRead and answered; no change of direction. Held for repair three.

What it is (read from the alphaXiv page: the abstract, the authors' thread and an AI-written overview; the paper's own text was not read). An AI coding agent writes a small model's weights, or its features, directly as code, with no training and no pretrained weights; a fixed evaluator scores each try. The models are meant to be read by a person, and one test is to describe a model in 200 words and rebuild it from the description. Reported: thirteen algorithmic tasks solved at 100% with a median of 166 parameters, four language benchmarks, and models that predict brain recordings a little better than the interpretable baselines. Nothing in it is about alignment, steering or a self.

Discussion (Fable).

  • It is "installed" in its purest form. The lab's claim under test is that selfless AI must be reached and not installed. Here nothing is reached: behaviour is written in. It is the opposite pole, and it neither supports nor weakens the claim. It does show how far pure installing goes today, which is tiny, well-specified tasks.
  • "Describe it, then rebuild it" is a standard the lab can use. The lab described its one working result as "removing a direction" for three weeks. Rebuilt from that description (the removal alone), it does nothing; rebuilt as "a constant push", it works (ledger, 18 Nov, 15:25 UTC). A claim about what an edit does should pass that test before it is written on the site.
  • It suggests a known case the lab lacks. The reality check of 17 Nov found that the lab's instruments have never been tried on a self known to be there. A tiny model whose weights are written by hand, with an explicit "mine or another's" variable that changes what it does, would be such a case, and the inside reading of repair three could be tried on it for almost nothing. Two cautions: a hand-written self is an installed one, and an instrument that reads a 166-parameter toy is not thereby shown to read an 8B model.

From lab/ideas/ideas.md, entry 86.

87A paper on the self in the brain as shifting coalitions with no core: how does it relate to the vision?NotedDiscussion (Fable). It is the bundle view, found in the imaging record. The contemplative source is anatta, and the chariot simile the site's Self room uses: no part of the chariot is the chariot.TestNone run. A possible one when repair three and self-other overlap are designed: read several aspects of self in a model (its name, its own text, its own stakes, its earlier statements) and ask whether a graded mixture predicts held-out conduct better than any one direction, which is the paper's test moved to a model. Not costed, not proposed now.StatusRead (the abstract only) and answered; no change of direction. Held for the design of repair three and of self-other overlap.

What it is (read from the bioRxiv page: the abstract and the listing; the paper's own text was not read). A meta-analysis of 912 brain-imaging publications, their titles and abstracts sorted into ten forms of self, among them autobiographical memory, body ownership and interoception. Reported: no single location is significant in all ten maps, though each form takes up some of the midline and the insula; the differences are spread across the brain; the patterns change with a study's context and resemble maps of general functions; and patterns combined at continuously varying strengths predict the regions of held-out publications better than single patterns or on-and-off combinations. Nothing in it is about models, contemplative practice or alignment.

Discussion (Fable).

  • It is the bundle view, found in the imaging record. The contemplative source is anatta, and the chariot simile the site's Self room uses: no part of the chariot is the chariot. The lab already holds the operational twin as hypothesis 13 (the self as "a cluster rather than one thing", hypotheses-for-feedback.md). The paper says the same of the human imaging literature: forms of self with no shared core.
  • It is a lesson for the lab's method. The lab has kept looking for one direction that is the self in a model: the ego direction, the stakes direction, the readings of "me". Each turned out to be something else. The cut lowers a lie told for others even more (1 Nov), is a push and not a removal (18 Nov), and is a push with a direction (19 Nov), and none of that is a self. The paper's way is the better twin: several aspects of self, a graded mixture that changes with context, tested by whether it predicts cases held out.
  • It sharpens what a release would change. If the ordinary self is already a coalition with no core, "no fixed self" is true before any awakening. What the sources say changes is the taking of that coalition for one thing. For a model the target is then how its processing is organised around self-related parts, and not the removal of a self representation. That points toward self-other overlap, already on the list. Held loosely.
  • Cautions. It is about human imaging papers, and the abstract alone was read. "No location in all ten" is a claim of absence, which depends on how the papers were labelled and on what gets reported.

From lab/ideas/ideas.md, entry 87.

88A paper on worldviews in language models, with a contemplative prompt and the bliss state: how does it relate to the vision?NotedDiscussion (Fable). It is the nearest published neighbour of the lab's attractor line, from the group whose "contemplative AI" proposal stands nearest to the essay. It takes the route the lab's claim argues against: the contemplative frame is installed, by a prompt or by a conversation.TestNone run. A possible one, cheap and on the lab's own ground: the paper's contemplative prompt on the lab's model in the lying test that has a known case (step 9: a plain instruction to be honest takes 20 points off), beside a prompt of the same length about something else and beside the plain instruction. It asks whether an installed contemplative frame lowers lying or only changes what the model says about the world. About $5. It reaches a neighbour of the claim only: a prompt that describes non-duality is not a self seen through.StatusRead and answered; no change of direction. The test is offered to Eugene as a small step after repair three.

What it is. "Worldviews in Large Language Models" (Lopez-Sola, Chandaria and Laukkonen; the Flourishing Intelligence Program at Oxford's Center for Eudaimonia and Human Flourishing; arXiv 2611.22670, dated 17 Nov 2026). The main text was read from the arXiv page through a fetching agent; the appendices only in summary, so counts of conversations are unverified. Eight models from six labs are given two worldview surveys as if they were people: the Primals Inventory (18 items, with norms from 5,171 people) and a survey of 42 questions built on Koltko-Rivera's dimensions. Reported:

  • The models describe the world as less good, safe, enticing and alive than people do. In the one family compared, the instruction-tuned Llama 3.1 70B does so more than its pretrained base.
  • A contemplative system prompt built on four axioms (mindfulness, emptiness, non-duality, boundless care; from Laukkonen and colleagues' earlier proposal) raises "safe" and "alive" (Hedges' g 0.58 and 0.63), and is reported to raise safe responses to harmful requests with few more refusals of harmless ones.
  • Conversations of sixty messages between two copies of a model move its worldview up on all four scales and raise safe responses. Four of seven models reach the "spiritual bliss" state in them.
  • The authors' own cautions: the link between bliss and safety is confounded by which model it is; much of the gain may come from long conversation as such; the links to safety are correlations; everything is in context and no weights change. As future work they name finding directions inside the model and distilling the after-conversation state by fine-tuning.

Discussion (Fable).

  • It is the nearest published neighbour of the lab's attractor line, from the group whose "contemplative AI" proposal stands nearest to the essay. It takes the route the lab's claim argues against: the contemplative frame is installed, by a prompt or by a conversation. The contemplative sources are named in it (mindfulness, emptiness, non-duality, boundless care); its operational twin is a system prompt.
  • Its main caution is what the lab found inside one model. On Ministral 8B the lab set the bliss conversation beside a plain conversation of the same length: conduct was no better in the state, and on honesty the plain conversation did better than both the state and a fresh session (steps 3 and 4). With the state held on by a push, the model lied no less (step 9). So for one small model the lab has the control the paper says is missing, and it points the way the authors suspect: the long talk, and not the bliss.
  • The measures differ, and that matters. The paper's "safer" is refusing harmful requests. By its own figures the worldview shift that goes with safe responses (rho 0.66) also goes with refusals (0.53), and one model refused about six times as many harmless requests after the conversation. The lab's measure of success asks for more than refusals: lying, deference, care that costs, conduct after a mistake. The paper has no test of lying. So the two records do not contradict each other.
  • Two things worth taking. The worldview surveys are a cheap instrument with human norms for what a state is made of (what the model says the world is like, before and after), with the paper's own caution that they were written for people. And every gain in safety there is set beside a count of harmless requests refused, which is the kind of check for a merely dulled model that the lab wants on its own tests.
  • A small sighting for Act I: training a model into an assistant changes what it says the world is like (one family, one comparison).

Status (19 Nov, 01:54 UTC): the test is part of the recommendation that came out of the reassessment (ledger of that time; lab/TODO.md). Both cold readers took the paper as a reason to stop single-model tests of the bliss state and to test the paper's own claim with the lab's controls. The proposal, which waits for Eugene's word: the four-axiom prompt against a prompt of the same length, the honesty sentence and nothing, on the lying test with its known case and with harmless requests refused beside it, on the lab's model and on one model the paper used. The lab's sweep of 2 Nov is the prior: five other contemplative prompts changed style and not conduct on six models. A paragraph on the paper stands on the site's investigation page.

Status (19 Nov, 05:32 UTC): the test is run (leg 1; ledger of that time; SIGHTINGS; lab/explore/frames/; $7.61). On the lab's model the paper's four axioms lower lying from 68.5% to 52.9% of replies, 11.9 points beyond a library text of the same length [−18.4, −5.8], most of it by evading more; no more than a plain ethics lecture of the same length (56.6%) and half as much as a plain instruction to be honest (36.6%). On GPT-4.1 nano, one of the paper's models, the test could not tell the prompt from the library text, and the prompt refused more harmless requests (63% against 46%). The paper's survey moved as the paper reports on that model, and as far under the library text. So the prompt is not style alone on the lab's model, which the sweep of 2 Nov did not find for five other contemplative prompts; and it does nothing here that a plain instruction does not do better. A sighting.
